## Learning objectives

- Produce and consume async streams
- Build producer/consumer pipelines with channels
- Choose between async and parallel processing

## Async streams

```csharp
public async IAsyncEnumerable<Customer> AllCustomersAsync([EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    string? continuation = null;
    do
    {
        var page = await _api.GetCustomersAsync(continuation, ct);
        foreach (var customer in page.Items) yield return customer;
        continuation = page.Next;
    } while (continuation is not null);
}

await foreach (var customer in client.AllCustomersAsync(ct))
{
    Console.WriteLine(customer.Name);
}
```

In .NET 10, the LINQ operators for `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` (`System.Linq.AsyncEnumerable`) are
part of the base libraries, so `WhereAwait`-style helpers from third-party packages are no longer
needed.

## Channels

```csharp
var channel = Channel.CreateBounded<Order>(new BoundedChannelOptions(100)
{
    FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait
});

var producer = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    await foreach (var order in ReadOrdersAsync(ct)) await channel.Writer.WriteAsync(order, ct);
    channel.Writer.Complete();
});

var consumer = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    await foreach (var order in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct)) await ProcessAsync(order, ct);
});

await Task.WhenAll(producer, consumer);
```

In ASP.NET Core, a channel registered as a singleton plus a `BackgroundService` reader is a
lightweight in-process work queue.

## Parallelism

```csharp
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(imageUrls, new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 4, CancellationToken = ct },
    async (url, token) =>
    {
        var bytes = await http.GetByteArrayAsync(url, token);
        await File.WriteAllBytesAsync(Path.Combine(dir, Path.GetFileName(url)), bytes, token);
    });
```

## Locks

```csharp
private readonly Lock _gate = new();

public void Increment()
{
    lock (_gate) { _count++; }
}
```

`System.Threading.Lock` is a dedicated lock type that the compiler recognises in `lock` statements.
For simple counters, `Interlocked.Increment(ref _count)` is cheaper still.

title: Memory, spans and measuring performance
questions:

      - id: view

        correct: true

      - text: A compressed array
      - text: A type that can be stored in a class field
    explanation: "`Span<T>` is a `ref struct`, so it lives on the stack and cannot be a field of a class, but it can slice memory with no allocations."
  - id: benchmark
    prompt: What is the recommended way to compare the performance of two implementations?
    options:
      - text: Wrap each in a `Stopwatch` and run it once in Debug mode
      - text: Count the lines of code
      - id: bdn
        text: Use BenchmarkDotNet in a Release build
        correct: true
    explanation: BenchmarkDotNet handles warm-up, JIT tiering, statistics and memory diagnostics.
  - id: alloc
    prompt: Which techniques reduce allocations on hot paths?
    type: multiple
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: Parsing slices with `ReadOnlySpan<char>` instead of `Substring`
        correct: true
      - text: Using `stackalloc` for small, fixed-size temporary buffers
        correct: true
      - text: Calling `GC.Collect()` after every request
    explanation: Pooling, slicing and stack allocation avoid garbage. Forcing collections usually makes performance worse.
---
## Learning objectives

- Use `Span<T>` and `Memory<T>` to avoid copying
- Pool buffers and use `stackalloc` safely
- Measure before optimising

## The cost of allocations

Every heap allocation eventually costs garbage-collection work. On hot paths — parsers,
serializers, middleware — allocation-free code can make a large difference. Everywhere else,
clarity wins.

## Spans

```csharp
public static class Csv
{
    public static int Sum(ReadOnlySpan<char> line)
    {
        var total = 0;
        foreach (var range in line.Split(','))
        {
            total += int.Parse(line[range]);
        }
        return total;
    }
}

Console.WriteLine(Csv.Sum("1,2,3,4"));
```

`MemoryExtensions.Split` (.NET 9) enumerates ranges without creating substrings, and
`int.Parse` accepts spans directly.

| Type | Lives | Use for |
|------|-------|---------|
| `Span<T>` / `ReadOnlySpan<T>` | Stack only (`ref struct`) | Synchronous slicing and parsing |
| `Memory<T>` / `ReadOnlyMemory<T>` | Heap-storable | Async APIs, fields |

## Pooling and stackalloc

```csharp
var buffer = ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Rent(64 * 1024);
try
{
    int read;
    while ((read = await stream.ReadAsync(buffer.AsMemory(), ct)) > 0)
        hasher.AppendData(buffer.AsSpan(0, read));
}
finally
{
    ArrayPool<byte>.Shared.Return(buffer);
}

Span<byte> small = stackalloc byte[16];
Random.Shared.NextBytes(small);
```

Keep `stackalloc` small (a few hundred bytes); large stack buffers risk stack overflow.

## Measure

```csharp
[MemoryDiagnoser]
public class ParsingBenchmarks
{
    private const string Line = "10,20,30,40,50";

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public int WithSplit() => Line.Split(',').Sum(int.Parse);

    [Benchmark]
    public int WithSpan() => Csv.Sum(Line);
}
```

```bash
dotnet run -c Release
```

Optimise only what a profiler or benchmark shows is slow, and keep the readable version when the
gain does not matter.

## The host

```csharp
var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);
builder.Services.AddHostedService<CleanupWorker>();
await builder.Build().RunAsync();
```

`WebApplication.CreateBuilder` is the same idea with the web server added. Both give you DI,
configuration, logging and graceful shutdown on Ctrl+C or SIGTERM.

## A background worker

```csharp
public sealed partial class CleanupWorker(
    IServiceScopeFactory scopes,
    TimeProvider time,
    ILogger<CleanupWorker> logger) : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        using var timer = new PeriodicTimer(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), time);
        while (await timer.WaitForNextTickAsync(stoppingToken))
        {
            await using var scope = scopes.CreateAsyncScope();
            var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ShopDbContext>();
            var removed = await db.Carts
                .Where(c => c.UpdatedAt < time.GetUtcNow().AddDays(-30))
                .ExecuteDeleteAsync(stoppingToken);
            LogRemoved(removed);
        }
    }

    [LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Information, Message = "Removed {Count} abandoned carts")]
    private partial void LogRemoved(int count);
}
```

## Registration patterns

```csharp
services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>();
services.AddSingleton<IShippingMethod, StandardShipping>();
services.AddSingleton<IShippingMethod, ExpressShipping>();      // IEnumerable<IShippingMethod> gets both
services.TryAddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>();                // only if not already registered
services.AddKeyedSingleton<ICache, MemoryCache>("local");
services.AddKeyedSingleton<ICache, RedisCache>("distributed");
```

```csharp
public sealed class CatalogService([FromKeyedServices("distributed")] ICache cache) { }
```

## Validation

In the Development environment, ASP.NET Core enables `ValidateScopes` and `ValidateOnBuild`, so
captive dependencies and missing registrations fail at startup. You can enable them for any host:

```csharp
builder.ConfigureContainer(new DefaultServiceProviderFactory(new ServiceProviderOptions
{
    ValidateScopes = true,

```

## Sources and precedence

`WebApplication.CreateBuilder` loads, in order (later wins):

1. `appsettings.json`
2. `appsettings.{Environment}.json`
3. User secrets (Development only)
4. Environment variables
5. Command-line arguments

```bash

dotnet run -- --Smtp:Port=2525
```

## Strongly typed options

```json
{
  "Smtp": { "Host": "smtp.example.com", "Port": 587, "From": "shop@example.com" }
}
```

```csharp
public sealed class SmtpOptions
{
    public const string Section = "Smtp";

    [Required] public required string Host { get; init; }
    [Range(1, 65535)] public int Port { get; init; } = 587;
    [Required, EmailAddress] public required string From { get; init; }
}

builder.Services.AddOptions<SmtpOptions>()
    .BindConfiguration(SmtpOptions.Section)
    .ValidateDataAnnotations()
    .ValidateOnStart();
```

`ValidateOnStart` turns a typo in configuration into a startup failure instead of a 3 a.m. bug.

```csharp
public sealed class SmtpEmailSender(IOptions<SmtpOptions> options) : IEmailSender
{
    private readonly SmtpOptions _options = options.Value;
}
```

## Choosing an interface

| Interface | Lifetime | Reloads | Use when |
|-----------|----------|---------|----------|
| `IOptions<T>` | Singleton | No | Settings fixed for the app's lifetime |
| `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` | Scoped | Per request | Per-request consistency with reload |
| `IOptionsMonitor<T>` | Singleton | Yes, with `OnChange` | Singletons that must see changes |

```csharp
public static class ShopTelemetry
{
```

## A first API

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IProductStore, InMemoryProductStore>();
```

## Feature-based endpoint modules

```csharp
public static class ProductEndpoints
{
    public static IEndpointRouteBuilder MapProductEndpoints(this IEndpointRouteBuilder routes)
    {
        var group = routes.MapGroup("/api/products").WithTags("Products");

        group.MapGet("/", ListAsync);
        group.MapGet("/{id:int}", GetAsync).WithName("GetProduct");
        group.MapPost("/", CreateAsync).RequireAuthorization("catalog-admin");

        return routes;
    }

    private static async Task<Ok<IReadOnlyList<Product>>> ListAsync(IProductStore store, CancellationToken ct) =>
        TypedResults.Ok(await store.ListAsync(ct));

    internal static async Task<Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>> GetAsync(int id, IProductStore store, CancellationToken ct) =>
        await store.FindAsync(id, ct) is { } product
            ? TypedResults.Ok(product)
            : TypedResults.NotFound();

    private static async Task<CreatedAtRoute<Product>> CreateAsync(CreateProduct request, IProductStore store, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var product = await store.AddAsync(request, ct);
        return TypedResults.CreatedAtRoute(product, "GetProduct", new { id = product.Id });
    }
}

public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name, decimal Price);
```

## Binding sources

| Parameter | Bound from |
|-----------|------------|
| Matches a route segment (`{id}`) | Route |
| Simple type not in the route | Query string |
| Complex type on POST/PUT | JSON body |
| Registered service | DI container |
| `HttpContext`, `CancellationToken`, `ClaimsPrincipal` | Special types |

Use `[FromQuery]`, `[FromHeader]`, `[FromBody]`, `[FromServices]` or `[AsParameters]` when you need
to be explicit.

## Testing handlers

Because handlers are ordinary static methods returning typed results, you can unit test them directly:

```csharp
var result = await ProductEndpoints.GetAsync(42, new InMemoryProductStore(), CancellationToken.None);
Assert.IsType<NotFound>(result.Result);
```

`GetAsync` is `internal`, so the test project needs `<InternalsVisibleTo Include="Shop.Api.Tests" />` in the API project file.

## Validation

```csharp
builder.Services.AddValidation();

public sealed class CreateProduct
{
    [Required, StringLength(100)]
    public required string Name { get; init; }

    [Range(0.01, 100_000)]
    public decimal Price { get; init; }
}
```

An invalid body now produces a `400 Bad Request` with a validation problem response, and the
handler never runs. Validation also applies to query and header parameters, and you can opt out
per endpoint with `.DisableValidation()`.

## OpenAPI


## Problem details everywhere

```csharp
builder.Services.AddProblemDetails();
builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<DomainExceptionHandler>();

app.UseExceptionHandler();
app.UseStatusCodePages();
```

```csharp
public sealed class DomainExceptionHandler(IProblemDetailsService problems) : IExceptionHandler
{
    public async ValueTask<bool> TryHandleAsync(HttpContext context, Exception exception, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var (status, title) = exception switch
        {
            NotFoundException => (StatusCodes.Status404NotFound, "Resource not found"),
            ConcurrencyException => (StatusCodes.Status409Conflict, "The resource was modified"),
            _ => (0, "")
        };
        if (status == 0) return false;

        context.Response.StatusCode = status;
        return await problems.TryWriteAsync(new ProblemDetailsContext
        {
            HttpContext = context,
            Exception = exception,
            ProblemDetails = { Title = title, Status = status }
        });
    }
}
```

Returning `false` passes unknown exceptions on to the default handler, which returns a generic
500 without leaking stack traces in production.

      - text: Per-attempt and total request timeouts
        correct: true
      - text: Automatic caching of every response for 24 hours
    explanation: The standard pipeline (built on Polly) combines a rate limiter, total timeout, retry, circuit breaker and attempt timeout.
---
## Learning objectives

- Order middleware correctly and write custom middleware
- Use `IHttpClientFactory` with typed clients
- Add resilience with the standard resilience handler

## The pipeline

```csharp
app.UseExceptionHandler();
app.UseHsts();
app.UseHttpsRedirection();
app.UseCors();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.UseRateLimiter();
app.MapProductEndpoints();
```

Each middleware can act before and after the next one. Order matters: exception handling first so
it wraps everything; authentication before authorization.

## Custom middleware

```csharp
public sealed class CorrelationIdMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
{
    private const string Header = "X-Correlation-Id";

    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        var id = context.Request.Headers[Header].FirstOrDefault() ?? Guid.CreateVersion7().ToString();
        context.Response.Headers[Header] = id;
        using (context.RequestServices.GetRequiredService<ILogger<CorrelationIdMiddleware>>()
                   .BeginScope(new Dictionary<string, object> { ["CorrelationId"] = id }))
        {
            await next(context);
        }
    }
}

app.UseMiddleware<CorrelationIdMiddleware>();
```

`Guid.CreateVersion7()` (.NET 9) creates time-ordered GUIDs that index well in databases.

## Typed HTTP clients

```csharp
public sealed class GitHubClient(HttpClient http)
{
    public Task<Repo?> GetRepoAsync(string owner, string name, CancellationToken ct) =>
        http.GetFromJsonAsync<Repo>($"repos/{owner}/{name}", ct);
}

builder.Services.AddHttpClient<GitHubClient>(c =>
{
    c.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.github.com/");
    c.DefaultRequestHeaders.UserAgent.ParseAdd("shop-api/1.0");
})
.AddStandardResilienceHandler();
```

## Resilience

Networks fail. The standard handler adds, from outermost to innermost:

1. Rate limiter
2. Total request timeout
3. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter
4. Circuit breaker
5. Per-attempt timeout

Retries are only safe for **idempotent** operations; for POSTs, use idempotency keys or disable
retries for that client.

## Caching

`HybridCache` (`Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Hybrid`) combines in-memory and distributed caching
with stampede protection:

```csharp
var product = await cache.GetOrCreateAsync($"product:{id}",
    async token => await store.FindAsync(id, token), cancellationToken: ct);
```

title: EF Core essentials
questions:
  - id: dbcontext-lifetime
    prompt: What is the recommended lifetime for a `DbContext` in an ASP.NET Core app?
    options:
      - text: Singleton, shared by all requests
      - text: Transient, created for every method call
      - text: Static field on the controller
      - id: scoped
        text: Scoped — one instance per request (the default of `AddDbContext`)
        correct: true
    explanation: A `DbContext` is a lightweight unit of work and is not thread-safe. Use one per request, or `IDbContextFactory<T>` for other scopes.
  - id: no-tracking
    prompt: When should you use `AsNoTracking()`?
    options:
      - id: read-only
        text: For read-only queries whose results you will not modify and save
        correct: true
      - text: Whenever you plan to call `SaveChanges` on the results
      - text: Only when using SQLite
    explanation: Skipping change tracking reduces memory and CPU for read-only data.
  - id: n-plus-one
    prompt: Which of these help avoid the N+1 query problem?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Projecting with `Select` into a DTO that includes the related data you need
        correct: true
      - text: Using `Include` to load related entities in the same query
        correct: true
      - text: Lazy loading related collections inside a `foreach` over the parent rows
      - text: Logging SQL during development to spot repeated queries
        correct: true
    explanation: Lazy loading inside loops is the classic cause of N+1. Projection and `Include` fetch related data up front; SQL logging reveals the problem.
  - id: migrations
    prompt: Which command creates a new migration from model changes?
    options:
      - text: "`dotnet ef database drop`"
      - id: add
        text: "`dotnet ef migrations add AddOrderStatus`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`dotnet ef dbcontext scaffold`"
    explanation: "`migrations add` generates a migration class; `database update` or a migration bundle applies it."
---
Entity Framework Core is .NET's full ORM. (For hand-written SQL with minimal overhead, see the
Dapper book on this site — many systems use both.)

## Learning objectives

- Configure a `DbContext` and map entities
- Write efficient queries with projection and no-tracking
- Manage schema changes with migrations

## A model and a context

```csharp
public sealed class Order
{
    public int Id { get; private set; }
    public required string CustomerEmail { get; init; }
    public OrderStatus Status { get; private set; } = OrderStatus.Pending;
    public List<OrderLine> Lines { get; } = [];
}

public sealed class ShopDbContext(DbContextOptions<ShopDbContext> options) : DbContext(options)
{
    public DbSet<Order> Orders => Set<Order>();

    protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder model)
    {
        model.Entity<Order>(o =>
        {
            o.Property(x => x.CustomerEmail).HasMaxLength(256);
            o.Property(x => x.Status).HasConversion<string>().HasMaxLength(20);
            o.HasMany(x => x.Lines).WithOne().OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Cascade);
        });
    }
}

builder.Services.AddDbContext<ShopDbContext>(o =>
    o.UseSqlServer(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Shop")));
```

## Query efficiently

```csharp
var summaries = await db.Orders
    .AsNoTracking()
    .Where(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Paid)
    .OrderByDescending(o => o.Id)
    .Select(o => new OrderSummary(o.Id, o.CustomerEmail, o.Lines.Sum(l => l.Quantity * l.UnitPrice)))
    .Take(50)
    .ToListAsync(ct);
```

Projection fetches only needed columns and computes the sum in SQL — one round trip, no N+1.

## Change tracking

```csharp
var order = await db.Orders.Include(o => o.Lines).SingleAsync(o => o.Id == id, ct);
order.MarkPaid();
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);   // EF detects the change and issues one UPDATE
```

## Bulk operations

```csharp
await db.Orders
    .Where(o => o.Status == OrderStatus.Pending && o.CreatedAt < cutoff)
    .ExecuteDeleteAsync(ct);
```

`ExecuteUpdateAsync` and `ExecuteDeleteAsync` run a single SQL statement without loading entities.

## Migrations

```bash
dotnet ef migrations add AddOrderStatus
dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent -o migrate.sql
dotnet ef migrations bundle -o efbundle
```

In production, prefer reviewed SQL scripts or migration bundles in the deployment pipeline over
calling `Database.Migrate()` at application startup.

## Learning objectives

- Use `LeftJoin` and `RightJoin` in queries
- Combine multiple named query filters
- Write conditional bulk updates

EF Core 10 is an LTS release that requires .NET 10.

## LeftJoin and RightJoin

```csharp
var report = await db.Customers
    .LeftJoin(db.Orders,
        customer => customer.Id,
        order => order.CustomerId,
        (customer, order) => new { customer.Name, OrderId = (int?)order.Id })
    .ToListAsync(ct);
```

## Named query filters

```csharp
model.Entity<Order>()
    .HasQueryFilter("SoftDelete", o => !o.IsDeleted)
    .HasQueryFilter("Tenant", o => o.TenantId == _tenant.Id);

var includingDeleted = await db.Orders
    .IgnoreQueryFilters(["SoftDelete"])   // the tenant filter still applies
    .ToListAsync(ct);
```

Previously, ignoring the soft-delete filter also removed tenant isolation — a dangerous trap.

## Conditional bulk updates

```csharp
await db.Products
    .Where(p => p.CategoryId == categoryId)
    .ExecuteUpdateAsync(setters =>
    {
        setters.SetProperty(p => p.UpdatedAt, now);
        if (newPrice is not null)
        {
            setters.SetProperty(p => p.Price, newPrice.Value);
        }
    }, ct);
```

Before EF Core 10 the argument had to be an expression tree, so conditional setters required
building expressions by hand.

## Other highlights

- **Complex types** improvements, including mapping complex types to JSON columns and optional complex types
- **Vector search** for SQL Server 2025 and Azure SQL (`SqlVector<float>` and `EF.Functions.VectorDistance`)
- Better translation of parameterised collections (`Contains` over a list)

> Upgrade tip: read the "breaking changes" page for each EF Core version before upgrading a
> production app; most are small but some change query translation.

---
title: SOLID with modern .NET building blocks
questions:
  - id: srp-tool
    prompt: Which .NET feature most directly supports the Dependency Inversion Principle?
    options:
      - text: Extension methods
      - text: Records
      - id: di
        text: Constructor injection with the built-in DI container and a composition root in `Program.cs`
        correct: true
      - text: The `dynamic` keyword
    explanation: Business classes depend on abstractions passed through constructors; only the composition root knows the concrete types.
  - id: ocp-tool
    prompt: Registering several `IShippingMethod` implementations and injecting `IEnumerable<IShippingMethod>` supports which principle?
    options:
      - text: Liskov Substitution — because the list is ordered
      - id: ocp
        text: Open/Closed — new implementations are added without modifying the consumer
        correct: true
      - text: Single Responsibility — because the container creates the objects
    explanation: The consumer is closed to modification yet the system is open to new shipping methods.
  - id: mapping
    prompt: Which pairings of .NET feature and principle are accurate?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: "`TimeProvider` — depend on an abstraction for a volatile dependency (DIP)"
        correct: true
      - text: "Decorating an `IHttpClientFactory` client with `DelegatingHandler`s — extend behaviour without editing the client (OCP)"
        correct: true
      - text: "`IReadOnlyList<T>` return types — give clients only the capability they need (ISP)"
        correct: true
      - text: "`static` service classes with global state — easier substitution (LSP)"
    explanation: Static global state prevents substitution entirely; it is the opposite of LSP-friendly design.
---
The SOLID book on this site covers each principle in depth. This section maps them onto the
everyday building blocks of modern .NET.

## Learning objectives

- Recognise SOLID in the features you already use
- Apply each principle with idiomatic .NET constructs

## The map

| Principle | Modern .NET building block |
|-----------|----------------------------|
| SRP | Feature folders; small handlers; `BackgroundService` per job; options classes per concern |
| OCP | `IEnumerable<T>` injection; middleware; `DelegatingHandler`; keyed services |
| LSP | Contract tests across implementations; `IReadOnly*` interfaces instead of throwing `NotSupportedException` |
| ISP | Small interfaces (`IOrderReader`, `IOrderWriter`); minimal API handlers asking only for what they use |
| DIP | Constructor injection; abstractions owned by the application layer; `TimeProvider`, `IHttpClientFactory` |

## DIP and OCP together

```csharp
public interface IPaymentProvider
{
    string Name { get; }
    Task<PaymentResult> ChargeAsync(PaymentRequest request, CancellationToken ct);
}

builder.Services.AddKeyedScoped<IPaymentProvider, StripeProvider>("stripe");
builder.Services.AddKeyedScoped<IPaymentProvider, AdyenProvider>("adyen");

app.MapPost("/pay/{provider}", async (string provider, PaymentRequest request,
    IServiceProvider services, CancellationToken ct) =>
{
    var payments = services.GetKeyedService<IPaymentProvider>(provider);
    return payments is null
        ? Results.NotFound()
        : Results.Ok(await payments.ChargeAsync(request, ct));
});
```

Resolving by key from `IServiceProvider` at the edge (an endpoint) is legitimate — the endpoint *is*
part of the composition layer. Business classes still receive their dependencies through constructors.

## Cross-cutting concerns as decorators

```csharp
public sealed class TimingHandler(ILogger<TimingHandler> logger) : DelegatingHandler
{
    protected override async Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(HttpRequestMessage request, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var start = Stopwatch.GetTimestamp();
        var response = await base.SendAsync(request, ct);
        logger.LogInformation("{Method} {Uri} took {Elapsed}", request.Method, request.RequestUri, Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(start));
        return response;
    }
}

builder.Services.AddTransient<TimingHandler>();
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<GitHubClient>().AddHttpMessageHandler<TimingHandler>();
```

The `GitHubClient` never changes; behaviour is layered around it.

title: Clean architecture and vertical slices
questions:
  - id: dependency-rule
    prompt: What is the dependency rule in clean architecture?
    options:
      - id: inward
        text: Source-code dependencies point only inward, toward the domain and application core
        correct: true
      - text: Outer layers must never reference inner layers
      - text: Every layer must reference every other layer
      - text: The database layer is the centre of the design
    explanation: The domain knows nothing about the web, databases or frameworks. Infrastructure depends on the core, not the reverse.
  - id: vertical-slice
    prompt: What characterises a vertical slice architecture?
    options:
      - id: feature
        text: Code is organised by feature, with each request's handler, validation and data access kept together
        correct: true
      - text: Code is organised by technical layer — all controllers together, all repositories together
      - text: Every feature is deployed as a separate microservice
    explanation: Slices maximise cohesion per feature; the code that changes together lives together.
  - id: project-refs
    prompt: In a clean architecture solution, which project references are correct?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Infrastructure references Application
        correct: true
      - text: Application references Domain
        correct: true
      - text: The Web project references Infrastructure (to compose it) and Application
        correct: true
      - text: Domain references Infrastructure to save entities
    explanation: The domain is at the centre and references nothing project-specific.
---
## Learning objectives

- Lay out a solution following the dependency rule
- Compare layered clean architecture with vertical slices
- Pick a structure that fits the size of the system

## Clean architecture layout

```text
src/
  Shop.Domain/          entities, value objects, domain events — no dependencies
  Shop.Application/     use cases, interfaces such as IOrderRepository — references Domain
  Shop.Infrastructure/  EF Core, Dapper, email, queues — references Application
  Shop.Web/             endpoints, composition root — references Application and Infrastructure
tests/
  Shop.Domain.Tests/
  Shop.Application.Tests/
  Shop.Web.IntegrationTests/
```

```csharp
// Shop.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs
public static class DependencyInjection
{
    public static IServiceCollection AddInfrastructure(this IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration config)
    {
        services.AddDbContext<ShopDbContext>(o => o.UseSqlServer(config.GetConnectionString("Shop")));
        services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, EfOrderRepository>();
        return services;
    }
}
```

The compiler enforces the dependency rule: `Shop.Domain` cannot call EF Core because it has no
reference to it.

## Vertical slices

```text
Features/
  Orders/
    PlaceOrder.cs       request, validator, handler, endpoint mapping
    CancelOrder.cs
    GetOrder.cs
```

```csharp
public static class PlaceOrder
{
    public sealed record Request(int CustomerId, IReadOnlyList<LineItem> Lines);
    public sealed record Response(int OrderId);

    public static void Map(IEndpointRouteBuilder app) =>
        app.MapPost("/orders", HandleAsync);

    private static async Task<Created<Response>> HandleAsync(Request request, ShopDbContext db, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = Order.Create(request.CustomerId, request.Lines);
        db.Orders.Add(order);
        await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
        return TypedResults.Created($"/orders/{order.Id}", new Response(order.Id));
    }
}
```

## Choosing

| Situation | Good fit |
|-----------|----------|
| Rich domain rules, long-lived system, several delivery mechanisms | Clean architecture |
| Mostly CRUD and queries, features change independently | Vertical slices |
| Small service or prototype | A single project with feature folders |

Many teams combine them: a rich `Domain` project at the centre and vertical slices in the
application layer. Whatever you choose, keep the domain free of infrastructure concerns.

## Unit tests with xUnit v3

```csharp
public class PricingTests
{
    [Theory]
    [InlineData(50, 0)]
```

## Integration tests

```csharp
public class OrderApiTests(WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    [Fact]
    public async Task Unknown_order_returns_404()
    {
        var client = factory.WithWebHostBuilder(b => b.ConfigureServices(services =>
        {
            services.RemoveAll<IOrderRepository>();
            services.AddSingleton<IOrderRepository, InMemoryOrderRepository>();
        })).CreateClient();

        var response = await client.GetAsync("/api/orders/999", TestContext.Current.CancellationToken);

        Assert.Equal(HttpStatusCode.NotFound, response.StatusCode);
    }
}
```

`WebApplicationFactory` needs a `public` `Program` class. In .NET 10 the Web SDK generates

## Real databases with Testcontainers

```csharp
public sealed class SqlServerFixture : IAsyncLifetime
{
    private readonly MsSqlContainer _container = new MsSqlBuilder().WithImage("mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest").Build();
    public string ConnectionString => _container.GetConnectionString();

    public async ValueTask InitializeAsync() => await _container.StartAsync();
    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync() => await _container.DisposeAsync();
}
```

xUnit v3's `IAsyncLifetime` uses `ValueTask`. Share one container per test class or collection to
keep runs fast.

title: Publishing, containers and Native AOT
questions:

    prompt: What is the main trade-off of Native AOT?
    options:
      - text: Smaller binaries but much slower steady-state performance than JIT in every case
      - id: tradeoff
        text: Much faster startup and lower memory, at the cost of restrictions on unbounded reflection and runtime code generation
        correct: true

    explanation: AOT compiles ahead of time and trims unused code, so features that discover code at runtime need source generators or annotations instead.

    explanation: Reflection-based serialization is not trim- or AOT-safe; the source generator produces the metadata at compile time.
  - id: options
    prompt: Which publish options exist in modern .NET?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Framework-dependent deployment, which relies on an installed runtime
        correct: true
      - text: Self-contained deployment, which bundles the runtime
        correct: true
      - text: Single-file publishing
        correct: true
      - text: ReadyToRun, which precompiles code to improve startup while keeping the JIT
        correct: true
    explanation: These options can be combined to balance size, startup time and compatibility.

## Learning objectives

- Choose between framework-dependent, self-contained, single-file and ReadyToRun
- Build container images with the SDK
- Decide when Native AOT is worth it

## Publish options

| Option | Property | Effect |
|--------|----------|--------|
| Framework-dependent | default | Small output; needs the runtime installed |
| Self-contained | `--self-contained` | Bundles the runtime for a specific RID |
| Single file | `PublishSingleFile` | One executable |
| Trimmed | `PublishTrimmed` | Removes unused code (self-contained only) |
| ReadyToRun | `PublishReadyToRun` | Precompiled code for faster startup, JIT still available |
| Native AOT | `PublishAot` | Fully native executable, no JIT |

```bash
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 --self-contained -p:PublishSingleFile=true
```

## Containers without a Dockerfile

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <ContainerRepository>shop-api</ContainerRepository>
  <ContainerImageTags>1.4.0;latest</ContainerImageTags>
</PropertyGroup>
```

```bash
dotnet publish -c Release -t:PublishContainer
docker run -p 8080:8080 shop-api:1.4.0
```

Since .NET 8, official images run as a non-root `app` user and ASP.NET Core listens on port 8080
by default. `ContainerFamily` can select smaller variants such as chiseled Ubuntu images.

## Native AOT

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
  <InvariantGlobalization>true</InvariantGlobalization>
</PropertyGroup>
```

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateSlimBuilder(args);
builder.Services.ConfigureHttpJsonOptions(o =>
    o.SerializerOptions.TypeInfoResolverChain.Insert(0, AppJsonContext.Default));

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapGet("/health", () => new HealthStatus("ok", DateTimeOffset.UtcNow));
app.Run();

public sealed record HealthStatus(string Status, DateTimeOffset At);

[JsonSerializable(typeof(HealthStatus))]
internal partial class AppJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext;
```

AOT apps start in milliseconds and use less memory — ideal for serverless functions, CLI tools and
dense container hosting. Libraries that rely on runtime reflection (some ORMs, older serializers,
dynamic proxies) may not be compatible; the build emits trim/AOT warnings that you should treat as
errors.

## Checklist before production

- Health checks (`AddHealthChecks`, `MapHealthChecks("/healthz")`)
- Structured logging and OpenTelemetry exporters configured
- Configuration validated at startup
- Secrets from a vault or managed identity, never from the image
- Graceful shutdown honoured (`stoppingToken`, request cancellation)

title: The evidence hierarchy
questions:
  - id: confounding
    prompt: A cohort study finds that people who eat more blueberries live longer. What is the most important reason this does not prove that blueberries extend life?
    options:
      - text: Cohort studies are always fraudulent
      - text: Blueberries contain no nutrients
      - id: confounders
        text: Blueberry eaters may differ in income, exercise, smoking and many other factors that also affect lifespan
        correct: true
      - text: Cohort studies cannot measure death
    explanation: This is **confounding**. Statistical adjustment helps but can never fully remove differences that were measured badly or not measured at all ("residual confounding").
  - id: rct-strength
    prompt: Why is a large randomised controlled trial (RCT) the strongest single design for testing whether a diet causes an outcome?
    options:
      - id: balances
        text: Random allocation balances known and unknown confounders between groups on average
        correct: true
      - text: RCTs never have dropouts
      - text: RCTs always last for decades
      - text: RCTs do not need statistics
    explanation: Randomisation is the only method that balances factors nobody has thought of. RCTs still have weaknesses — short duration, poor adherence, and unrepresentative participants.
  - id: rct-limits
    prompt: Which are genuine limitations of diet RCTs?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Chronic diseases take decades to develop, but most diet trials last months to a few years
        correct: true
      - text: Participants often drift back to their usual diet, shrinking the difference between groups
        correct: true
      - text: Blinding is usually impossible because people know what they are eating
        correct: true
      - text: Randomisation makes the results apply to every population on Earth automatically
    explanation: Randomisation buys internal validity, not universal generalisability. Adherence and duration are the chronic weak points of nutrition RCTs.
  - id: self-report
    prompt: What have doubly labelled water studies revealed about self-reported food intake?
    options:
      - text: People report their intake almost perfectly
      - text: People systematically over-report how much they eat
      - id: under
        text: People systematically under-report energy intake, and the error is larger in people with higher body weight
        correct: true
    explanation: Doubly labelled water measures true energy expenditure. Comparisons show substantial, non-random under-reporting, which is one reason food-frequency questionnaires are a weak measurement tool.
  - id: mechanistic
    prompt: A compound kills cancer cells in a Petri dish. What can you conclude about eating foods that contain it?
    options:
      - text: The food prevents cancer
      - text: The food cures cancer
      - id: almost-nothing
        text: Almost nothing yet — dose, absorption, metabolism and whole-body effects are untested
        correct: true
      - text: The food is dangerous
    explanation: Bleach also kills cancer cells in a dish. In-vitro findings generate hypotheses; they are the bottom of the evidence pyramid for human health claims.
  - id: mr
    prompt: What does Mendelian randomisation use as a natural experiment?
    options:
      - text: Random selection of foods in supermarkets
      - id: genes
        text: Genetic variants, randomly assigned at conception, that affect exposure to a nutrient or risk factor
        correct: true
      - text: Random weather patterns that affect crop yields
    explanation: Because genes are allocated randomly at conception, they are less confounded by lifestyle. The method has its own assumptions (for example, that the gene affects the outcome only through the exposure).
  - id: meta
    prompt: A meta-analysis pools twenty small, biased trials. What is the result?
    options:
      - text: A highly reliable answer, because twenty is a large number
      - id: precise-biased
        text: A precise estimate of a biased answer — pooling does not remove shared bias
        correct: true
      - text: An answer that is always null
    explanation: Garbage in, garbage out. Good meta-analyses assess risk of bias in each study and check for publication bias.

## Learning objectives

- Rank study designs by the strength of causal evidence they provide
- Explain confounding, reverse causation and measurement error
- Recognise why diet research is unusually hard

## Why nutrition science seems to change its mind

Headlines flip between "coffee kills" and "coffee saves lives" because most nutrition headlines come
from **observational** studies, which find associations, not causes. The underlying science moves far
more slowly than the headlines. Some conclusions — that vitamin C prevents scurvy, that folic acid
prevents neural tube defects, that trans fats raise heart disease risk, that excess energy intake causes
weight gain — are as solid as anything in biology. Others — the ideal ratio of fats, the health effect
of a single food — remain open.

## The hierarchy, from weakest to strongest

| Design | What it can show | Main weakness |
|--------|------------------|---------------|
| Anecdote, testimonial, tradition | That something happened to someone | No comparison, no control for chance or bias |
| In-vitro (cell) and animal studies | Plausible mechanisms | Doses and biology often do not translate to humans |
| Cross-sectional survey | Associations at one point in time | Cannot tell which came first |
| Case-control study | Associations with rare diseases | Recall bias: sick people remember diets differently |
| Prospective cohort | Associations over years, with exposure measured before disease | Confounding and measurement error |
| Mendelian randomisation | Causal estimates using genetic "natural experiments" | Assumptions about pleiotropy can fail |
| Randomised controlled trial | Cause and effect | Short, small, poor adherence, often unblinded |
| Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs | The overall weight of trial evidence | Only as good as the trials it pools |

Evidence is strongest when **different designs with different weaknesses agree**. The case that smoking
causes lung cancer, and that LDL cholesterol causes atherosclerosis, rests on exactly this
convergence: cohorts, trials, genetics and mechanisms all point the same way.

## The three classic traps

**Confounding.** People who eat more vegetables also tend to smoke less, exercise more and earn more.
Adjusting for measured factors helps; unmeasured ones remain.

**Reverse causation.** People who have just been diagnosed with heart disease often change their diet.
A study might then wrongly conclude that the "healthy" diet is linked with heart disease.

**Measurement error.** Most cohort studies ask people what they ate over the past year using a
food-frequency questionnaire. Doubly labelled water studies show that people under-report energy
intake, typically by hundreds of calories per day, and not randomly.

## Why diet is harder than drugs

- You cannot give a placebo steak; blinding is rarely possible
- Changing one nutrient changes others (cutting fat raises carbohydrate or protein)
- Effects are usually small and take decades to show
- Food is eaten in patterns, not as isolated nutrients
- Funding is limited compared with drug trials, so many trials are small and short

## The multiple-comparisons problem

Schoenfeld and Ioannidis took 50 common ingredients from a cookbook and searched the literature:
40 of them had been studied for cancer risk, and most of those had published associations — some
claiming increased risk, some decreased, often for the same food. Most single studies reporting a
single food–cancer association show implausibly large effects that shrink in meta-analyses.

> **Rule of thumb:** a single observational study about a single food is a hypothesis, not a finding.

## Sources

- Schoenfeld JD, Ioannidis JPA. Is everything we eat associated with cancer? *Am J Clin Nutr* 2013. [doi:10.3945/ajcn.112.047142](https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.112.047142)
- Ioannidis JPA. The challenge of reforming nutritional epidemiologic research. *JAMA* 2018.
- Satija A, Yu E, Willett WC, Hu FB. Understanding nutritional epidemiology and its role in policy. *Adv Nutr* 2015.
- Ference BA et al. LDL causes atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (EAS consensus). *Eur Heart J* 2017. [doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehx144](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehx144)

questions:
  - id: absolute
    prompt: Eating 50 g of processed meat daily is associated with about an 18% higher relative risk of colorectal cancer. If lifetime risk is about 5%, roughly what does the risk become?
    options:
      - text: About 23%
      - id: six
        text: About 6%
        correct: true
      - text: About 18%
      - text: About 50%
    explanation: An 18% **relative** increase on a 5% baseline is about 0.9 percentage points (5% × 1.18 ≈ 5.9%). Both numbers are true; the absolute number is what matters for an individual decision.
  - id: nnt
    prompt: A treatment reduces risk of an event from 2% to 1% over five years. Which statements are correct?
    type: multiple

        correct: true
      - text: The absolute risk reduction is 1 percentage point
        correct: true
      - text: About 100 people need to be treated for five years to prevent one event
        correct: true
      - text: Half of all treated people avoid the event because of the treatment
    explanation: Number needed to treat = 1 / absolute risk reduction = 1 / 0.01 = 100. Headlines usually quote the relative figure because it sounds bigger.
  - id: grades
    prompt: In this book, what does the label **Uncertain** mean?
    options:
      - text: The claim is false
      - id: mixed
        text: The evidence is mixed or weak, and reasonable experts disagree
        correct: true
      - text: The claim is proven by multiple large RCTs
      - text: Nobody has ever studied the claim
    explanation: Uncertain is not a polite word for wrong. It means we genuinely do not know yet. Not supported is the label for claims the evidence contradicts or has failed to support.
  - id: nature

      - text: Ad hominem
      - text: Straw man
      - id: appeal-nature
        text: Appeal to nature
        correct: true
      - text: Survivorship bias
    explanation: Arsenic, botulinum toxin, aflatoxin and deadly nightshade are all natural. Pasteurisation, vaccines and water treatment are not "natural" and save millions of lives.
  - id: tradition

        correct: true
      - text: It must work, or people would have stopped using it
      - text: It is at least safe
    explanation: The appeal to tradition ignores that pre-scientific societies had no way to separate real effects from placebo, natural recovery and chance.
  - id: red-flags

    type: multiple

        correct: true

        correct: true

      - text: Claims that "doctors don't want you to know" this
        correct: true

  - id: funding

  - id: hazard-risk

## Learning objectives

- Convert relative risks into absolute risks
- Use the four evidence grades applied throughout this book
- Spot the common rhetorical tricks in diet marketing

## The evidence grades used in this book

| Grade | Meaning | Typical basis |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| **Established** | We are as sure as science gets; reversal would be astonishing | Consistent RCTs, or overwhelming agreement across trials, cohorts, genetics and mechanism |
| **Strong** | Very likely true; details may change | Consistent cohort evidence with supporting trials or mechanisms |
| **Uncertain** | Mixed or weak evidence; reasonable experts disagree | Inconsistent studies, small trials, or observational data only |
| **Not supported** | Evidence contradicts the claim, or there is none despite looking | Null or harmful trials, implausible mechanisms |

These grades describe the **evidence**, not the popularity, tradition, religious status or political
alignment of a claim.

## Relative versus absolute risk

A relative risk (RR) of 1.18 means 18% more events than the comparison group. Whether that matters
depends on how common the event is.

| Baseline risk | RR 1.18 | Absolute increase |
|---------------|---------|-------------------|
| 1 in 1,000 | 1.18 in 1,000 | 0.018 percentage points |
| 5 in 100 | 5.9 in 100 | 0.9 percentage points |
| 30 in 100 | 35.4 in 100 | 5.4 percentage points |

**Number needed to treat (NNT)** is 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction. It answers "how many people must make
this change for one to benefit?"

## Hazard is not risk

The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies **hazards** by the strength of the
evidence that something *can* cause cancer, not by *how much* cancer it causes. Group 1 contains tobacco,
alcohol, processed meat, solar radiation and plutonium. Their risks differ by orders of magnitude.

## Rhetorical tricks to recognise

| Trick | Example | Why it fails |
|-------|---------|--------------|
| Appeal to nature | "Raw is how nature intended" | Many natural things are lethal; many artificial ones save lives |
| Appeal to tradition or sanctity | "Ancient texts say this animal's urine heals" | Age and religious status are not evidence |
| Appeal to authority | "A doctor recommends it" | One person's opinion is not a body of evidence |
| Cherry-picking | Citing one positive trial out of twelve | The weight of evidence matters |
| Moving the goalposts | "The trial used the wrong dose" after every null result | An unfalsifiable claim is not scientific |
| Conspiracy | "Big Pharma hides the cure" | Real effective cheap treatments (aspirin, ORS, folic acid) are promoted, not hidden |
| Chemophobia | "You can't pronounce it, so don't eat it" | Pronounceability is not toxicity; a banana contains dozens of hard-to-pronounce compounds |

## Conflicts of interest cut every way

Kearns and colleagues (2016) documented that the Sugar Research Foundation funded a 1967 review in the
*New England Journal of Medicine* that downplayed sugar's role in heart disease. Industry funding is a
real source of bias. So is selling supplements, books, courses, raw milk or "detox" teas. Treat
everyone's financial and ideological interests the same way.

## Sources

- Kearns CE, Schmidt LA, Glantz SA. Sugar industry and coronary heart disease research. *JAMA Intern Med* 2016. [doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2016.5394](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2016.5394)
- Bouvard V et al. Carcinogenicity of consumption of red and processed meat. *Lancet Oncol* 2015. [doi:10.1016/S1470-2045(15)00444-1](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1470-2045(15)00444-1)
- Guyatt GH et al. GRADE: an emerging consensus on rating quality of evidence. *BMJ* 2008.

        correct: true
      - text: No — calories do not matter if you eat the right foods

        correct: true
      - text: No fat loss on either diet

  - id: adaptive

    options:

        correct: true
      - text: All contestants had kept the weight off
    explanation: "Adaptive thermogenesis is real. Its size in typical, slower weight loss is smaller and debated. Most contestants regained much of the weight."
  - id: pontzer

    options:

        correct: true

    explanation: Middle-age weight gain is therefore not mainly explained by a "slowing metabolism"; changes in intake and activity matter more.
  - id: hadza

  - id: pound

## Learning objectives

- Describe the components of energy expenditure
- Explain why energy balance is true but not the whole story
- Understand metabolic adaptation and its limits

## The calorie

A kilocalorie (kcal, the "Calorie" on food labels) is the energy needed to raise 1 kg of water by 1 °C.
Food labels use the **Atwater factors**:

| Macronutrient | kcal per gram |
|---------------|---------------|
| Carbohydrate | 4 |
| Protein | 4 |
| Fat | 9 |
| Alcohol | 7 |
| Fibre | about 2 (varies) |

These are averages. Whole almonds, for example, deliver fewer calories than labels claim because some fat
stays trapped in cell walls.

## Where energy goes

| Component | Share of total, typical sedentary adult |
|-----------|----------------------------------------|
| Resting metabolic rate (organs, maintaining body temperature) | 60–70% |
| Thermic effect of food (digestion and processing) | about 10% (protein highest, fat lowest) |
| Physical activity — exercise plus non-exercise activity (NEAT) | 20–30%, highly variable |

## What is certain

- **Established:** body fat changes only when energy intake differs from expenditure. This is the first law
  of thermodynamics applied to a living system; no diet has escaped it in a metabolic ward
- **Established:** expenditure falls when weight falls, both because a smaller body costs less to run and
  because of adaptive changes
- **Strong:** appetite rises during weight loss (higher ghrelin, lower leptin), which makes maintenance hard
- **Uncertain:** the existence and strength of a defended "set point" for body weight

## The carbohydrate–insulin model

This model claims that refined carbohydrate raises insulin, which traps fat in fat cells, causing hunger and
lowered expenditure. It is a legitimate hypothesis that was tested directly. Hall's metabolic-ward studies
(2015, 2016) found no fat-loss advantage of low-carbohydrate diets at equal calories, and the large
DIETFITS trial (2018) found no difference in weight loss between healthy low-fat and healthy low-carbohydrate
diets over 12 months, and no effect of baseline insulin secretion. Its proponents dispute aspects of these
trials. Grade: **Not supported** as a primary explanation of obesity; low-carbohydrate diets remain a valid
*tool* for people who find them easier.

## Metabolic adaptation

Participants in *The Biggest Loser* had resting metabolic rates about 500 kcal/day below prediction six years
later. That was extreme, rapid weight loss. In more typical weight loss the adaptation is smaller — tens to
low hundreds of kcal/day — and its long-term size is still debated.

## Energy expenditure across life

Pontzer et al. (2021), using doubly labelled water data on 6,421 people, found size-adjusted expenditure is
highest in infancy, declines through childhood, is stable from about 20 to 60, and declines thereafter.

## Sources

- Hall KD et al. Calorie for calorie, dietary fat restriction results in more body fat loss than carbohydrate restriction. *Cell Metab* 2015. [doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2015.07.021](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2015.07.021)
- Fothergill E et al. Persistent metabolic adaptation 6 years after "The Biggest Loser" competition. *Obesity* 2016. [doi:10.1002/oby.21538](https://doi.org/10.1002/oby.21538)
- Pontzer H et al. Daily energy expenditure through the human life course. *Science* 2021. [doi:10.1126/science.abe5017](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abe5017)
- Pontzer H et al. Hunter-gatherer energetics and human obesity. *PLoS One* 2012.
- Ludwig DS et al. The carbohydrate-insulin model: a physiological perspective. *Am J Clin Nutr* 2021.

## Learning objectives

- Compare popular diets on the evidence
- Understand why maintenance is the hard part

## Diets compared

| Claim | Grade | Notes |
|-------|-------|-------|
| Any diet that creates a sustained energy deficit produces weight loss | **Established** | Metabolic-ward and long-term trials |
| Low-carb beats low-fat for long-term weight loss | **Not supported** | DIETFITS and meta-analyses: small or no difference beyond 12 months |
| Low-carb diets can help people with type 2 diabetes lower blood glucose | **Strong** | Short-term glycaemic benefits; long-term data weaker |
| Higher-protein diets help preserve muscle and increase satiety during weight loss | **Strong** | Modest effects |
| Ultra-processed diets promote overeating | **Strong but limited** | One small ward RCT plus cohorts (see the processed-food section) |
| Blood type, metabolic type or "genetic" diets beat generic advice | **Not supported** | No trial benefit |
| Meal replacements improve short-term weight loss | **Strong** | Used successfully in DiRECT and Look AHEAD |

## The individual variation problem

In DIETFITS, average loss was about 5–6 kg in both arms, but individuals ranged from losing more than 25 kg
to gaining 10 kg. Averages hide the fact that the best diet for an individual is the one they can keep.

## Drugs

GLP-1 receptor agonists and related drugs changed obesity treatment:

| Drug | Trial | Mean weight loss vs placebo |
|------|-------|----------------------------|
| Semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly injection | STEP 1 (2021) | about 14.9% vs 2.4% at 68 weeks |
| Tirzepatide 15 mg weekly injection | SURMOUNT-1 (2022) | about 20.9% vs 3.1% at 72 weeks |

Oral options followed: an oral semaglutide product for weight management was approved in the US in
late 2025, and orforglipron (Foundayo), a small-molecule oral GLP-1 agonist, in April 2026.

- **Established:** large average weight loss while taking them
- **Established:** semaglutide reduced major cardiovascular events by about 20% in SELECT
- **Established:** most weight is regained after stopping (STEP 1 extension)
- **Uncertain:** long-term (decades) safety; best strategies for preserving muscle; effects of lifelong use

Common side effects are nausea, vomiting, constipation and diarrhoea. Adequate protein and resistance
training are sensible during drug-induced weight loss, because some of the weight lost is lean tissue.

## Surgery

The Swedish Obese Subjects study and others show sustained weight loss, remission of type 2 diabetes in many
patients, and lower mortality. Lifelong supplementation (B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D) is required after
most procedures.

## Sources

- Gardner CD et al. Effect of low-fat vs low-carbohydrate diet on 12-month weight loss (DIETFITS). *JAMA* 2018. [doi:10.1001/jama.2018.0245](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.0245)
- Wilding JPH et al. Once-weekly semaglutide in adults with overweight or obesity (STEP 1). *NEJM* 2021. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2032183](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2032183)
- Jastreboff AM et al. Tirzepatide once weekly for the treatment of obesity (SURMOUNT-1). *NEJM* 2022. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2206038](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2206038)
- Lincoff AM et al. Semaglutide and cardiovascular outcomes in obesity without diabetes (SELECT). *NEJM* 2023. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2307563](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307563)
- Sjöström L et al. Effects of bariatric surgery on mortality in Swedish obese subjects. *NEJM* 2007.
- Wang J et al. ABO genotype, "blood-type diet" and cardiometabolic risk factors. *PLoS One* 2014.
- Rubino F et al. Definition and diagnostic criteria of clinical obesity. *Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol* 2025.

title: Carbohydrates and fibre
questions:
  - id: essential
    prompt: Is dietary carbohydrate an essential nutrient in the strict sense?
    options:
      - text: Yes — without it you die within weeks
      - id: not-strictly
        text: No — the body can make the glucose it needs from protein and glycerol, although carbohydrate-containing foods supply fibre and many nutrients
        correct: true
      - text: Yes — the brain can only use glucose
    explanation: The brain can run largely on ketones during prolonged carbohydrate restriction, and the liver makes glucose (gluconeogenesis). Essential nutrients are those the body cannot make, such as certain amino acids, two fatty acids, vitamins and minerals.
  - id: reynolds
    prompt: The 2019 Lancet meta-analysis by Reynolds and colleagues linked higher fibre intake with which outcomes?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Lower all-cause mortality
        correct: true
      - text: Lower coronary heart disease and stroke
        correct: true
      - text: Lower type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer
        correct: true
      - text: Higher body weight in trials
    explanation: People eating 25–29 g/day had 15–30% lower risks than those eating the least, with dose-response suggesting more is better. Trials showed lower body weight, blood pressure and cholesterol.
  - id: fibre-ai
    prompt: What is the US Adequate Intake for fibre?
    options:
      - text: 5 g per day
      - id: per-1000
        text: 14 g per 1,000 kcal — about 25 g for women and 38 g for men
        correct: true
      - text: 100 g per day
    explanation: Most adults in the US and UK eat around 15–20 g/day, well short of the target.
  - id: whole-grain
    prompt: What distinguishes a whole grain from a refined grain?
    options:
      - text: Whole grains have been bleached
      - id: bran-germ
        text: Whole grains keep the bran and germ as well as the starchy endosperm
        correct: true
      - text: Refined grains contain more fibre
    explanation: Refining removes most fibre, B vitamins, minerals and phytochemicals. Fortification adds back some vitamins and iron but not fibre.
  - id: gi
    prompt: What is the evidence grade for choosing foods by glycaemic index (GI) to improve health in people without diabetes?
    options:
      - text: Established
      - id: uncertain
        text: Uncertain — GI varies with ripeness, cooking and what else is eaten, and trial benefits beyond fibre and whole foods are small and inconsistent
        correct: true
      - text: Not supported — GI is meaningless
    explanation: GI is a real property of foods, but watermelon has a high GI and ice cream a low one — a reminder that GI alone is a poor guide to a healthy diet.
  - id: soluble

    options:
      - id: ldl
        text: Modest lowering of LDL cholesterol
        correct: true
      - text: Curing diabetes
      - text: Raising LDL cholesterol
    explanation: About 3 g/day of oat beta-glucan lowers LDL by roughly 5–10%, which is why regulators permit a health claim for it.
  - id: starch-rs
    prompt: What is resistant starch?
    options:
      - text: Starch that is toxic
      - id: escapes
        text: Starch that escapes digestion in the small intestine and is fermented in the colon, as found in cooled cooked potatoes and rice, legumes and green bananas

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish sugars, starches and fibres
- Know the fibre evidence and targets
- Understand the limits of glycaemic index

## Types of carbohydrate

| Type | Examples | Digestion |
|------|----------|-----------|
| Sugars (mono- and disaccharides) | Glucose, fructose, sucrose, lactose | Rapid |
| Starches | Grains, potatoes, legumes | Rapid to slow depending on structure |
| Resistant starch | Legumes, cooled cooked starch, green bananas | Fermented in the colon |
| Fibre | Cellulose, pectin, beta-glucan, inulin | Not digested by human enzymes; partly fermented by bacteria |

## Targets

- Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (US National Academies): **45–65%** of energy from carbohydrate
- Fibre: **14 g per 1,000 kcal** (US Adequate Intake); **30 g/day** for adults (UK SACN)
- WHO (2023) recommends adults eat at least 25 g/day of naturally occurring fibre and at least 400 g/day of
  fruit and vegetables

Healthy populations have thrived on diets ranging from about 10% to 80% carbohydrate. The **quality**
of carbohydrate matters more than the amount for most chronic-disease outcomes.

## What is known

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Higher fibre intake is associated with lower mortality, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer | **Strong** |
| Whole grains in place of refined grains reduce cardiometabolic risk | **Strong** |
| Viscous soluble fibre lowers LDL modestly | **Established** |
| Fibre improves constipation | **Established** for many fibres, notably psyllium |
| Carbohydrate itself causes obesity | **Not supported** |
| Low-GI diets add benefit beyond whole-food, high-fibre diets | **Uncertain** |
| "Net carbs" on labels are a regulated, meaningful metric | **Not supported** — the term has no FDA definition |

## Sources

- Reynolds A et al. Carbohydrate quality and human health: a series of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. *Lancet* 2019. [doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31809-9)
- Institute of Medicine. *Dietary Reference Intakes for Energy, Carbohydrate, Fiber, Fat, Fatty Acids, Cholesterol, Protein, and Amino Acids.* National Academies Press, 2005.
- WHO. Carbohydrate intake for adults and children: WHO guideline. 2023.
- Whitehead A et al. Cholesterol-lowering effects of oat beta-glucan: a meta-analysis. *Am J Clin Nutr* 2014.

title: Sugar and sweeteners
questions:

        correct: true
      - text: Sugar causes ADHD

      - text: Higher intake is associated with higher type 2 diabetes risk
        correct: true
      - text: Sugars, especially frequently consumed, cause dental caries
        correct: true
      - text: A single soda causes immediate diabetes
    explanation: Dental caries is the most firmly established harm of sugar. The weight and diabetes evidence comes from cohorts and trials and is strong for drinks.

    options:

      - id: dose
        text: No — harms are dose-dependent and mostly mediated by excess calories and dental effects; small amounts within a healthy diet have no demonstrated harm
        correct: true
    explanation: Calling sugar a toxin sounds scientific but is rhetoric. Excess free sugar is a genuine public-health problem; "any amount is poison" is not supported.
  - id: addiction

      - id: uncertain

        correct: true
      - text: Not studied
    explanation: Liking sweet tastes is innate. Whether some people show clinically meaningful food addiction is an open research question.
  - id: aspartame

  - id: who-nss

## Learning objectives

- Define free and added sugars
- Separate genuine harms of sugar from exaggerations
- Assess sweeteners with appropriate uncertainty

## Definitions

- **Free sugars (WHO):** sugars added by manufacturers, cooks or consumers, plus sugars naturally present in
  honey, syrups, fruit juices and fruit-juice concentrates
- **Added sugars (US):** similar, but excludes 100% fruit juice

## Targets

| Body | Recommendation |
|------|----------------|
| WHO (2015) | Free sugars below 10% of energy; below 5% for further benefit (conditional) |
| US Dietary Guidelines 2020–2025 | Added sugars below 10% of energy |
| US Dietary Guidelines 2025–2030 | No more than 10 g added sugar per meal for adults; none for young children |
| American Heart Association | Below 25 g/day for most women, 36 g/day for most men |

A single 330 ml can of cola contains about 35 g of sugar.

## The evidence

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Free sugars cause dental caries | **Established** |
| Sugar-sweetened drinks promote weight gain | **Strong** |
| Sugar-sweetened drinks increase type 2 diabetes risk independent of weight | **Strong** (observational, consistent) |
| Sugar causes hyperactivity in children | **Not supported** |
| Sugar "feeds cancer", so cancer patients must avoid all sugar | **Not supported** — all cells use glucose; the body regulates blood glucose regardless of diet |
| Whole fruit is harmful because of its sugar | **Not supported** |
| Honey or "unrefined" sugars are healthier than table sugar | **Not supported** in any meaningful way |
| Approved sweeteners at normal intakes cause cancer | **Not supported**; long-term effects remain **Uncertain** |

## Sugar and cancer

Cancer cells take up glucose avidly (which is how PET scans work), but so do brain and muscle. Dietary sugar
does not selectively feed tumours; blood glucose is held in a narrow range. Excess sugar can contribute to
obesity, which is a cause of at least 13 cancers — that indirect link is real.

## Sweeteners

Approved sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, acesulfame-K, saccharin, steviol glycosides, erythritol and
others) are assessed with an acceptable daily intake (ADI) set 100 times below the dose that caused no
effect in animals. Open questions include effects on the gut microbiome, and an observational link between
erythritol blood levels and cardiovascular events (Witkowski 2023) that needs confirmation.

## Sources

- WHO. Guideline: sugars intake for adults and children. 2015.
- Wolraich ML et al. The effect of sugar on behavior or cognition in children: a meta-analysis. *JAMA* 1995. [doi:10.1001/jama.1995.03530200053037](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1995.03530200053037)
- Malik VS, Hu FB. The role of sugar-sweetened beverages in the global epidemics of obesity and chronic diseases. *Nat Rev Endocrinol* 2022.
- WHO/IARC/JECFA. Aspartame hazard and risk assessment results released. 14 July 2023.
- WHO. Use of non-sugar sweeteners: WHO guideline. 2023.
- Witkowski M et al. The artificial sweetener erythritol and cardiovascular event risk. *Nat Med* 2023. [doi:10.1038/s41591-023-02223-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-023-02223-9)

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish fatty-acid types and their effects on blood lipids
- Understand the substitution principle
- Separate fish from fish-oil supplements

## Types of fat

| Type | Main sources | Effect on LDL when replacing carbohydrate |
|------|--------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Saturated (SFA) | Butter, cheese, fatty meat, palm and coconut oil | Raises |
| Monounsaturated (MUFA) | Olive oil, canola oil, avocados, nuts | Slightly lowers |
| Polyunsaturated omega-6 (PUFA) | Sunflower, soybean, corn oil, walnuts | Lowers |
| Polyunsaturated omega-3 | ALA in flax, chia, walnuts; EPA/DHA in oily fish | Neutral on LDL; EPA/DHA lower triglycerides |
| Industrial trans | Partially hydrogenated oils (now banned in many countries) | Raises LDL, lowers HDL |
| Ruminant trans | Small amounts in dairy and beef | Small effect at normal intakes |

## Targets

- Total fat: **20–35%** of energy (US AMDR); WHO says 30% or less to prevent unhealthy weight gain
- Saturated fat: **below 10%** of energy (WHO; US Dietary Guidelines, including 2025–2030)
- Trans fat: **below 1%** of energy (WHO), ideally industrial trans fat eliminated

## The evidence

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| LDL cholesterol causes atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease | **Established** |
| SFA raises LDL relative to unsaturated fats | **Established** |
| Replacing SFA with PUFA reduces cardiovascular events | **Strong** |
| Industrial trans fats increase heart disease | **Established** |
| Eating oily fish once or twice a week is associated with lower cardiac death | **Strong** |
| Fish-oil supplements prevent heart disease in healthy people | **Not supported** by the largest trials |
| Seed oils are toxic or inflammatory at normal intakes | **Not supported** |
| Dairy fat in cheese and yoghurt behaves differently from butter (the "food matrix") | **Uncertain** — intriguing, mostly observational |
| Butter and beef tallow are healthy cooking fats | **Not supported** — they are high in SFA and raise LDL compared with vegetable oils |

## A note on the 2025–2030 US guidelines

The 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans (January 2026) kept the under-10% saturated-fat limit while
featuring butter, beef tallow and full-fat dairy in their graphic. Researchers at Harvard and the Center for
Science in the Public Interest pointed out that following the food recommendations could exceed the
saturated-fat limit. Science does not change because a graphic changes.

- Mozaffarian D et al. Trans fatty acids and cardiovascular disease. *NEJM* 2006. [doi:10.1056/NEJMra054035](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMra054035)
- Neelakantan N et al. The effect of coconut oil consumption on cardiovascular risk factors. *Circulation* 2020. [doi:10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.119.043052](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.119.043052)
- Marklund M et al. Biomarkers of dietary omega-6 fatty acids and incident cardiovascular disease and mortality. *Circulation* 2019. [doi:10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.118.038908](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.118.038908)
- Ramsden CE et al. Re-evaluation of the traditional diet-heart hypothesis (Minnesota Coronary Experiment). *BMJ* 2016. [doi:10.1136/bmj.i1246](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i1246)

    options:
      - id: high-target
        text: 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day; critics note that most Americans already meet their protein needs and that the guidelines do not clearly prefer plant sources over red and processed meat
        correct: true
      - text: 0.4 g/kg/day; critics say it is too low for anyone to survive
      - text: No target; critics say protein should be banned
    explanation: Higher intakes can help older adults and people losing weight. Source matters; the long-term health effects of protein foods differ (legumes, fish and nuts versus processed meat).
  - id: older
    prompt: Why do expert groups such as PROT-AGE suggest more protein (about 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day) for adults over 65?
    options:
      - id: anabolic-resistance
        text: Ageing muscle responds less to protein (anabolic resistance), and sarcopenia increases frailty and falls
        correct: true
      - text: Older people cannot digest carbohydrate
      - text: Protein reverses ageing
    explanation: This is **Strong** for preventing deficiency-related muscle loss, but best results come from protein combined with resistance exercise.
  - id: source-matters
    prompt: Which substitution is associated with lower mortality in large cohorts?
    options:
      - text: Replacing plant protein with processed meat
      - id: plant
        text: Replacing red and processed meat protein with plant protein (legumes, nuts, soy, whole grains)
        correct: true
      - text: Replacing all protein with sugar
    explanation: This is observational (**Strong** but not Established); it is consistent across many cohorts and supported by effects on LDL and blood pressure.
---
## Learning objectives

- Know protein requirements across life stages
- Understand protein quality
- Evaluate high-protein claims

## Requirements

| Group | Suggested intake | Grade |
|-------|------------------|-------|
| Healthy adults (RDA) | 0.8 g/kg/day | **Established** as the minimum |
| Older adults | 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day (PROT-AGE, ESPEN) | **Strong** |
| Resistance-trained adults seeking muscle gain | about 1.6 g/kg/day, up to 2.2 | **Strong** |
| Endurance athletes | 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day | **Strong** |
| Pregnancy | about 1.1 g/kg/day or +25 g/day | **Established** |
| Chronic kidney disease (not on dialysis) | often restricted; individualised | Clinical guidance |

The US Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range is **10–35%** of energy.

## Protein quality

Protein quality depends on essential amino acid content and digestibility, scored by PDCAAS or the newer
DIAAS. Animal proteins and soy score highest. Plant-based diets easily meet needs when they include legumes
and enough energy.

## Claims

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Higher protein aids satiety and preserves lean mass during weight loss | **Strong** |
| Protein beyond about 1.6 g/kg/day adds muscle for most people | **Not supported** |
| High protein damages healthy kidneys | **Not supported** |
| High protein causes osteoporosis by leaching calcium | **Not supported** — higher protein is neutral or slightly positive for bones |
| Plant protein is "incomplete" and inadequate | **Not supported** for varied diets |
| Protein source affects disease risk | **Strong** (observational, consistent) |
| You can only absorb 20–30 g of protein per meal | **Not supported** — absorption is near-complete; a 2023 study found a 100 g dose produced a larger, longer anabolic response |

## Sources

- Morton RW et al. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains. *Br J Sports Med* 2018. [doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjsports-2017-097608)
- Bauer J et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people (PROT-AGE). *J Am Med Dir Assoc* 2013.
- Song M et al. Association of animal and plant protein intake with all-cause and cause-specific mortality. *JAMA Intern Med* 2016.
- Trommelen J et al. The anabolic response to protein ingestion during recovery from exercise has no upper limit. *Cell Rep Med* 2023.
- Center for Science in the Public Interest. What changed in the new dietary guidelines and why it matters. January 2026.

title: Vitamins and the deficiency diseases

        correct: true

      - text: Vitamin B12 — megaloblastic anaemia and neurological damage
        correct: true
    explanation: Night blindness is a sign of vitamin A deficiency. Scurvy is vitamin C deficiency.
  - id: goldberger
    prompt: In the early 20th century many experts believed pellagra was infectious. How did Joseph Goldberger challenge this?
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: He found the pellagra bacterium
      - text: He showed it was genetic
    explanation: Pellagra was linked to maize-heavy diets. Traditional Mesoamerican nixtamalisation (cooking maize with lime) releases bound niacin — a case where tradition happened to be right, which science then explained.
  - id: b12
    prompt: Who must take a reliable source of vitamin B12, such as a supplement or fortified foods?
    type: multiple

        correct: true
      - text: People on long-term metformin or acid-suppressing drugs may need monitoring
        correct: true
      - text: People who eat spirulina, because it contains active B12

  - id: fat-soluble

    options:

        correct: true

      - text: Only vitamin C
    explanation: Preformed vitamin A in high doses is teratogenic, so pregnant women should avoid high-dose vitamin A supplements and liver in large amounts. Water-soluble vitamins can also cause harm in excess — for example, B6 above about 100 mg/day long-term causes nerve damage.
  - id: vit-c-colds
