## Learning objectives

- Connect each vitamin to its deficiency disease and food sources
- Know who genuinely needs supplements
- Recognise toxicity limits

## History in brief

Nutrition science grew out of deficiency diseases: scurvy (vitamin C), beriberi (thiamin), pellagra (niacin),
rickets (vitamin D) and pernicious anaemia (B12). These are among the most **Established** findings in all of
medicine — each has a known molecule, mechanism, cure and prevention.

## The vitamins

| Vitamin | Main roles | Good sources | Deficiency |
|---------|-----------|--------------|------------|
| A (retinol; beta-carotene) | Vision, immunity, epithelia | Liver, dairy, orange and dark-green vegetables | Night blindness, xerophthalmia, infection deaths |
| D | Calcium absorption, bone | Sunlight on skin, oily fish, fortified foods | Rickets, osteomalacia |
| E | Antioxidant in membranes | Vegetable oils, nuts, seeds | Rare; neuropathy |
| K | Blood clotting, bone proteins | Leafy greens; K2 in fermented foods | Bleeding (especially newborns) |
| C | Collagen synthesis, antioxidant | Citrus, peppers, berries, potatoes | Scurvy |
| B1 thiamin | Carbohydrate metabolism | Whole grains, pork, legumes | Beriberi; Wernicke encephalopathy in alcohol use disorder |
| B2 riboflavin | Energy metabolism | Dairy, eggs, meat | Cracked lips, sore tongue |
| B3 niacin | Energy metabolism | Meat, fish, peanuts; made from tryptophan | Pellagra |
| B6 | Amino-acid metabolism | Poultry, fish, potatoes, bananas | Anaemia, neuropathy |
| Folate (B9) | DNA synthesis | Leafy greens, legumes, fortified grains | Megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects |
| B12 | DNA synthesis, nerve myelin | Animal foods, fortified foods | Anaemia, irreversible nerve damage |
| Biotin, pantothenic acid | Metabolism | Widespread | Very rare |

## Selected reference values (US, adults)

| Nutrient | RDA or AI | Tolerable upper limit (UL) |
|----------|-----------|----------------------------|
| Vitamin A | 700 µg RAE (women), 900 µg (men) | 3,000 µg preformed retinol |
| Vitamin D | 15 µg (600 IU); 20 µg (800 IU) over 70 | 100 µg (4,000 IU) |
| Vitamin C | 75 mg (women), 90 mg (men); +35 mg for smokers | 2,000 mg |
| Folate | 400 µg DFE; 600 µg in pregnancy | 1,000 µg from supplements and fortification |
| B12 | 2.4 µg | None set |
| B6 | 1.3–1.7 mg | 100 mg |

## Sources

- Institute of Medicine. *Dietary Reference Intakes* series, 1997–2011; National Academies.
- Hemilä H, Chalker E. Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2013. [doi:10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4)
- Imdad A et al. Vitamin A supplementation for preventing morbidity and mortality in children from six months to five years of age. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2022.
- Carpenter KJ. *The History of Scurvy and Vitamin C.* Cambridge University Press, 1986.
- CDC. Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in infants.

## Learning objectives

- Know the minerals of greatest public-health importance
- Understand salt reduction evidence
- Identify populations at risk of mineral deficiencies

## Major and trace minerals

| Mineral | Role | Sources | Notes |
|---------|------|---------|-------|
| Sodium | Fluid balance, nerve signals | Salt; mostly processed and restaurant food | Excess raises blood pressure |
| Potassium | Fluid balance, blood pressure | Vegetables, fruit, legumes, potatoes, dairy | Most people eat too little |
| Calcium | Bone, muscle, nerves | Dairy, fortified plant milks, tofu set with calcium, leafy greens | RDA 1,000 mg, 1,200 mg for women over 50 and men over 70 |
| Magnesium | Enzyme cofactor | Nuts, seeds, whole grains, legumes | Deficiency symptoms rare in healthy people |
| Iron | Oxygen transport | Meat, fish, legumes, fortified cereals | RDA 8 mg men; 18 mg women 19–50; 27 mg pregnancy |
| Zinc | Immunity, growth | Meat, shellfish, legumes, seeds | Deficiency stunts growth in children worldwide |
| Iodine | Thyroid hormones | Iodised salt, dairy, seafood | 150 µg adults; 220 µg pregnancy |
| Selenium | Antioxidant enzymes | Brazil nuts, seafood, grains | Narrow margin; a few Brazil nuts a day can exceed the UL |
| Fluoride | Tooth enamel | Fluoridated water, toothpaste | Prevents caries; excess causes fluorosis |

## Salt: what is known

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Reducing sodium lowers blood pressure | **Established** (DASH-Sodium and many trials) |
| High blood pressure causes stroke and heart disease | **Established** |
| Reducing sodium reduces cardiovascular events | **Strong** (SSaSS and modelling; long-term outcome trials are few) |
| Very low sodium (below about 1.5 g) is harmful | **Uncertain** — the J-shaped curves in some cohorts are likely affected by reverse causation and measurement error |

## Learning objectives

- Know the landmark supplement trials
- Identify who benefits from specific supplements
- Understand how supplements are regulated

## The antioxidant story

Observational studies in the 1980s found people eating more fruit and vegetables — and with higher blood
antioxidant levels — had less cancer and heart disease. The hypothesis that antioxidants explained this was
tested in large RCTs:

| Trial | Supplement | Result |
|-------|-----------|--------|
| ATBC (1994) | Beta-carotene | 18% more lung cancer in smokers |
| CARET (1996) | Beta-carotene + vitamin A | 28% more lung cancer; stopped early |
| HOPE (2000) / HOPE-TOO | Vitamin E | No cardiovascular benefit; possible heart failure increase |
| SELECT (2011) | Vitamin E, selenium | 17% more prostate cancer with vitamin E |
| Physicians' Health Study II (2012) | Multivitamin | Small (8%) reduction in total cancer; no cardiovascular benefit |
| VITAL (2019) | Vitamin D3, omega-3 | No reduction in primary cancer or cardiovascular outcomes |
| B-vitamin homocysteine trials (2006 onwards) | Folate, B6, B12 | Lowered homocysteine, no reduction in heart attacks |

Lesson: **a biomarker or an association is not an outcome**.

## Vitamin D, specifically

- **Established:** vitamin D prevents and treats rickets and osteomalacia
- **Established:** supplementation is appropriate for people at risk of deficiency (dark skin at high latitudes,
  little sun exposure, covered skin, breastfed infants, older adults in care homes)
- **Not supported:** routine high-dose vitamin D to prevent cancer, heart disease, depression, or fractures in
  people who are not deficient
- **Uncertain:** effects on cancer mortality; benefits in specific subgroups; optimal blood level (the US
  National Academies consider 20 ng/mL, 50 nmol/L, sufficient for most people)
- Toxicity (hypercalcaemia) occurs with chronic very high doses, usually above 10,000 IU/day

## Supplements with real evidence for specific groups

| Supplement | Who | Grade |
|-----------|-----|-------|
| Folic acid 400 µg | Anyone who could become pregnant | **Established** |
| B12 | Vegans; many older adults | **Established** |
| Iron | Diagnosed iron deficiency; often in pregnancy | **Established** |
| Vitamin D | Breastfed infants; people at risk of deficiency | **Established** |
| Iodine | Pregnancy and breastfeeding where diet is low (many guidelines suggest 150 µg) | **Strong** |
| Creatine | Athletes in strength and power sports | **Strong** |
| Calcium + vitamin D | Older adults in institutional care | **Strong** for fracture reduction in this group |

## Sources

- Alpha-Tocopherol, Beta Carotene Cancer Prevention Study Group. *NEJM* 1994. [doi:10.1056/NEJM199404143301501](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199404143301501)
- Omenn GS et al. Effects of a combination of beta carotene and vitamin A on lung cancer (CARET). *NEJM* 1996.
- Klein EA et al. Vitamin E and the risk of prostate cancer (SELECT). *JAMA* 2011.
- Manson JE et al. Vitamin D supplements and prevention of cancer and cardiovascular disease (VITAL). *NEJM* 2019. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1809944](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1809944)
- LeBoff MS et al. Supplemental vitamin D and incident fractures in midlife and older adults. *NEJM* 2022. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2202106](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2202106)
- Bjelakovic G et al. Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2012. [doi:10.1002/14651858.CD007176.pub2](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD007176.pub2)
- US Preventive Services Task Force. Vitamin, mineral, and multivitamin supplementation to prevent cardiovascular disease and cancer. *JAMA* 2022.
- Demay MB et al. Vitamin D for the prevention of disease: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. *J Clin Endocrinol Metab* 2024.

        correct: true
    explanation: Caffeine is a mild diuretic, but tolerance develops quickly and the fluid in the drink more than compensates.
  - id: hyponatraemia
    prompt: What is exercise-associated hyponatraemia?
    options:
      - text: Dehydration from not drinking enough
      - id: overdrinking
        text: Dangerously low blood sodium, mainly from drinking more fluid than is lost during long events — it has caused deaths in marathon runners
        correct: true
      - text: A deficiency of potassium
    explanation: Drinking to thirst is the safer strategy for most endurance athletes.
  - id: urine
    prompt: Which statements about urine colour are accurate?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Pale yellow generally indicates adequate hydration
        correct: true
      - text: B-vitamin supplements can turn urine bright yellow regardless of hydration
        correct: true
      - text: Completely clear urine all day means you must keep drinking more
    explanation: Persistently clear urine usually means you are drinking more than you need.
  - id: alkaline-water
    prompt: What is the evidence grade for claims that alkaline or "structured" water improves health?
    options:
      - text: Established
      - id: not-supported
        text: Not supported — stomach acid neutralises it and the body tightly regulates blood pH
        correct: true
      - text: Strong
    explanation: Blood pH is held between 7.35 and 7.45 by the lungs, kidneys and buffers. Food and water do not change it in healthy people.
---
## Learning objectives

- Estimate fluid needs realistically
- Recognise over-hydration as a real risk
- Dismiss hydration myths

## What is known

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Thirst is a reliable guide for healthy adults in normal conditions | **Strong** |
| Older adults have a blunted thirst response and are at greater risk of dehydration | **Strong** |
| Eight glasses a day is a requirement | **Not supported** |
| Tea and coffee count towards fluid intake | **Established** |
| Over-drinking during endurance events can kill | **Established** |
| Drinking more water aids weight loss | **Uncertain** — small trials show modest effects, mostly by replacing sugary drinks |
| Alkaline, hydrogen or "structured" water has health benefits | **Not supported** |
| Bottled water is safer than treated municipal tap water | **Not supported** in countries with regulated water supplies |

## Safe drinking water

Treated drinking water, chlorination and sanitation are among the largest public-health advances in history.
Unsafe water still causes hundreds of thousands of diarrhoeal deaths each year (WHO). "Raw water" (untreated
spring water) marketed as healthier carries the same pathogen risks that water treatment was invented to
remove.

## Sources

- National Academies. *Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate.* 2005.
- Valtin H. "Drink at least eight glasses of water a day." Really? Is there scientific evidence for "8 × 8"? *Am J Physiol* 2002.
- Hew-Butler T et al. Statement of the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference. *Clin J Sport Med* 2015.
- Killer SC et al. No evidence of dehydration with moderate daily coffee intake. *PLoS One* 2014.
- Fenton TR, Huang T. Systematic review of the association between dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer. *BMJ Open* 2016. [doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010438](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010438)

title: Alcohol
questions:
  - id: iarc
    prompt: How does IARC classify alcoholic beverages?
    options:
      - text: Group 3, not classifiable
      - text: Group 2B, possibly carcinogenic
      - id: group1
        text: Group 1, carcinogenic to humans
        correct: true
    explanation: Alcohol causes cancers of the mouth, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus, liver, colorectum and female breast. Acetaldehyde, its metabolite, damages DNA.
  - id: breast
    prompt: Is there a threshold below which alcohol does not increase breast cancer risk?
    options:
      - text: Yes, below three drinks a day
      - id: no-threshold
        text: No clear threshold has been identified; risk rises from low intakes, about 7–10% per daily drink
        correct: true
      - text: Alcohol lowers breast cancer risk
    explanation: The US Surgeon General's January 2025 advisory highlighted that alcohol is the third leading preventable cause of cancer in the US after tobacco and obesity.
  - id: j-curve
    prompt: Why is the "moderate drinking protects the heart" J-curve now doubted?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Non-drinker groups often include former drinkers who quit because of illness ("sick quitter" bias)
        correct: true
      - text: Moderate drinkers tend to be wealthier and healthier in other ways
        correct: true
      - text: Mendelian randomisation studies generally do not show a protective effect
        correct: true
      - text: Large RCTs have proven that wine prevents heart attacks
    explanation: No long-term RCT has tested moderate drinking on hard outcomes; the NIH-funded MACH15 trial was cancelled in 2018 after revelations of industry funding solicitation. Grade for cardioprotection - **Uncertain**, leaning **Not supported**.
  - id: standard-drink
    prompt: How much pure alcohol is in a US "standard drink"?
    options:
      - text: 5 g
      - id: fourteen
        text: 14 g
        correct: true
      - text: 50 g
    explanation: That is roughly 355 ml of 5% beer, 150 ml of 12% wine or 45 ml of 40% spirits. A UK unit is 8 g; definitions differ by country.
  - id: pregnancy
    prompt: What is the guidance on alcohol in pregnancy?
    options:
      - text: One glass of wine a day is beneficial
      - id: none-safe
        text: No safe amount has been established, so avoiding alcohol entirely is recommended
        correct: true
      - text: Only spirits are harmful
    explanation: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders are entirely preventable. Low-level exposure effects are harder to measure, which is exactly why the advice is abstention.
  - id: resveratrol
    prompt: Red wine contains resveratrol. Is that a reason to drink it for health?
    options:
      - text: Yes, the resveratrol outweighs the alcohol
      - id: tiny-dose
        text: No — the amounts are tiny compared with doses used in animal studies, human trials are disappointing, and alcohol's harms are established
        correct: true
    explanation: You would need to drink hundreds of litres of wine to match some animal-study doses.
  - id: gbd
    prompt: The Global Burden of Disease alcohol analysis (Lancet 2018) concluded that the level of drinking that minimised overall health loss was what?
    options:
      - id: zero
        text: Zero standard drinks per week
        correct: true
      - text: Two drinks per day
      - text: Seven drinks per day
    explanation: A 2022 GBD update found small net benefits for some older adults with high cardiovascular risk, but recommended zero for people aged 15–39. Estimates of very-low-dose effects remain debated; harms at higher intakes are not.
  - id: dga-alcohol
    prompt: How did the 2025–2030 US Dietary Guidelines change alcohol advice compared with 2020–2025?
    options:
      - text: They recommended a daily glass of wine
      - id: vaguer
        text: They dropped the numeric limits (up to 2 drinks a day for men, 1 for women) in favour of a general "drink less" message
        correct: true
      - text: They banned alcohol
    explanation: Critics noted that removing numbers made the advice vaguer, while the cancer evidence had become stronger.
---
## Learning objectives

- Understand alcohol's established harms
- Evaluate the "moderate drinking is healthy" claim
- Know standard drink sizes

## What is established

| Effect | Grade |
|--------|-------|
| Causes at least seven cancers | **Established** |
| Liver disease (fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis) | **Established** |
| Raises blood pressure and causes atrial fibrillation with dose | **Established** |
| Causes fetal alcohol spectrum disorders | **Established** |
| Injury, violence and road deaths | **Established** |
| Addiction (alcohol use disorder) | **Established** |
| Light drinking protects the heart | **Uncertain** — likely overstated by confounding |
| Any amount is safe for cancer | **Not supported** |
| Red wine is a health food | **Not supported** |

## Harm rises with dose

There is a broad consensus that **less is better**. In 2023 the WHO Regional Office for Europe stated that no
safe level of alcohol consumption for cancer has been identified. That is a statement about cancer risk;
total health effects at very low intakes are smaller and harder to measure, and scientists continue to argue
about them. The direction of advice is not in doubt.

## Sources

- IARC Monographs volume 100E. Alcohol consumption and ethyl carbamate. 2012.
- GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators. Alcohol use and burden for 195 countries and territories. *Lancet* 2018. [doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31310-2](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31310-2)
- GBD 2020 Alcohol Collaborators. Population-level risks of alcohol consumption by amount, geography, age, sex, and year. *Lancet* 2022.
- US Surgeon General. Alcohol and Cancer Risk advisory. January 2025.
- Stockwell T et al. Do "moderate" drinkers have reduced mortality risk? A systematic review and meta-analysis. *J Stud Alcohol Drugs* 2016.
- Millwood IY et al. Conventional and genetic evidence on alcohol and vascular disease aetiology (China Kadoorie Biobank). *Lancet* 2019.

title: Caffeine, coffee and tea
questions:
  - id: limit
    prompt: What daily caffeine intake do the FDA and EFSA consider generally not associated with adverse effects in healthy adults?
    options:
      - text: 50 mg
      - id: four-hundred
        text: Up to about 400 mg
        correct: true
      - text: 2,000 mg
    explanation: That is roughly four cups of brewed coffee. Sensitivity varies; pregnancy guidance (ACOG, EFSA) is below 200 mg/day.
  - id: half-life
    prompt: What is the typical half-life of caffeine in healthy adults?
    options:
      - text: 10 minutes
      - id: hours
        text: About 3–7 hours, longer in pregnancy and with some medications
        correct: true
      - text: Three days
    explanation: Caffeine in the afternoon can still affect sleep at bedtime, even in people who feel they fall asleep easily.
  - id: coffee-mortality
    prompt: What do large cohort studies generally find about moderate coffee drinking (about 2–4 cups/day)?
    options:
      - text: Strongly increased mortality
      - id: lower
        text: Associations with lower all-cause mortality, type 2 diabetes and liver disease
        correct: true
      - text: No studies exist
    explanation: Grade - **Strong** for "not harmful" in most adults; **Uncertain** for "causes benefit", since the data are observational. Unfiltered coffee (French press, boiled) contains cafestol, which raises LDL; paper filters remove most of it.
  - id: energy-drinks
    prompt: What is the main concern about energy drinks for adolescents?
    options:
      - id: dose-sugar
        text: High caffeine doses per can, often combined with large amounts of sugar and rapid consumption
        correct: true
      - text: They contain no caffeine
      - text: They are illegal everywhere
    explanation: Several countries restrict sales to minors. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that energy drinks have no place in children's diets.
  - id: lethal
    prompt: Where do most fatal caffeine poisonings come from?
    options:
      - text: Ordinary coffee drinking
      - id: powders
        text: Pure caffeine powders and tablets, where a single teaspoon can contain several grams
        correct: true
      - text: Green tea
    explanation: The FDA warned in 2018 that bulk pure caffeine products are dangerous and took action against them.
  - id: tea
    prompt: Which statement about green tea extract supplements is accurate?
    options:
      - text: They are always safe because tea is natural
      - id: liver
        text: High-dose green tea extract supplements have been linked to cases of liver injury
        correct: true
      - text: They cure cancer
    explanation: Drinking tea as a beverage is associated with neutral to favourable outcomes. Concentrated extracts are a different dose — another reason "natural" is not the same as safe.
---
## Learning objectives

- Know safe caffeine intakes
- Interpret coffee research appropriately

## Caffeine content (approximate)

| Drink | Caffeine |
|-------|----------|
| Brewed coffee, 240 ml | 80–120 mg |
| Espresso, single shot | about 60–75 mg |
| Black tea, 240 ml | 40–60 mg |
| Green tea, 240 ml | 25–45 mg |
| Cola, 355 ml | 30–40 mg |
| Energy drink, 250 ml | about 80 mg (larger cans 150–300 mg) |

## Evidence summary

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Up to about 400 mg/day is safe for most healthy adults | **Strong** |
| Caffeine improves alertness and endurance performance | **Established** |
| Coffee causes heart disease in the general population | **Not supported** |
| Moderate coffee lowers type 2 diabetes risk | **Strong** association, causality **Uncertain** |
| Coffee "stunts growth" | **Not supported** |
| High caffeine in pregnancy is linked to lower birth weight | **Strong** association; hence the 200 mg limit |
| Caffeine withdrawal is real (headache, fatigue) | **Established** |

## Sources

- EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products. Scientific opinion on the safety of caffeine. *EFSA J* 2015.
- US FDA. Spilling the beans: how much caffeine is too much? 2018 (updated).
- Poole R et al. Coffee consumption and health: umbrella review of meta-analyses. *BMJ* 2017.
- van Dam RM, Hu FB, Willett WC. Coffee, caffeine, and health. *NEJM* 2020.
- ACOG Committee Opinion 462. Moderate caffeine consumption during pregnancy. 2010 (reaffirmed).

title: Dietary patterns — Mediterranean, DASH, plant-based and ketogenic
questions:
  - id: predimed

        text: About a 30% relative reduction in major cardiovascular events
        correct: true
      - text: No difference
      - text: A 90% reduction in all deaths
    explanation: The 2013 paper was retracted and reanalysed because some sites did not randomise properly; the reanalysis gave similar results. This illustrates science correcting itself in public.
  - id: dash

    options:
      - text: Cause rapid weight loss
      - id: bp
        text: Lower blood pressure
        correct: true
      - text: Treat epilepsy
    explanation: DASH is rich in vegetables, fruit, low-fat dairy, whole grains, nuts and legumes, and low in red meat and sweets. In controlled feeding trials it lowered blood pressure within two weeks, and more so combined with lower sodium.
  - id: keto-epilepsy

    options:
      - text: Cancer cure
      - id: epilepsy
        text: Drug-resistant epilepsy, especially in children
        correct: true
      - text: Autism cure
    explanation: Ketogenic diets have been used for epilepsy since the 1920s and have RCT support. Claims for curing cancer are **Not supported**.
  - id: keto-ldl
    prompt: Which are recognised effects or risks of ketogenic diets?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Substantial LDL cholesterol increases in some people
        correct: true
      - text: Short-term side effects such as fatigue and headaches ("keto flu")
        correct: true
      - text: Lower intake of fibre-rich foods unless carefully planned
        correct: true
      - text: Guaranteed superior long-term weight loss
    explanation: Some people, often lean and active, show very large LDL rises on ketogenic diets. Long-term weight loss is similar to other diets with equal adherence.
  - id: vegan-needs

    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Vitamin B12
        correct: true
      - text: Iodine
        correct: true
      - text: Calcium and vitamin D
        correct: true
      - text: Omega-3 (EPA/DHA; algal oil is a vegan source)
        correct: true
      - text: Vitamin C
    explanation: Vitamin C is abundant in plant foods. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics considers appropriately planned vegetarian and vegan diets healthful for all life stages, with B12 supplementation essential for vegans.
  - id: carnivore

    options:

        correct: true

  - id: blue-zones

  - id: common-ground
    prompt: Which features are shared by nearly all dietary patterns associated with good health?
    options:

## Learning objectives

- Describe the main evidence-based dietary patterns
- Recognise the trade-offs of restrictive patterns
- Identify the common core of healthy diets

## Why patterns

People eat foods in combinations, so studying whole patterns avoids some pitfalls of single-nutrient research.
Pattern trials are also more realistic about what people can do.

## Patterns compared

| Pattern | Core features | Best evidence | Grade |
|---------|--------------|---------------|-------|
| Mediterranean | Olive oil, vegetables, legumes, fish, nuts, whole grains, moderate dairy | PREDIMED, Lyon Diet Heart, CORDIOPREV | **Strong** for cardiovascular benefit |
| DASH | Vegetables, fruit, low-fat dairy, low sodium | DASH and DASH-Sodium feeding trials | **Established** for blood-pressure lowering |
| Vegetarian / vegan | No meat (and for vegans no animal products) | Cohorts (Adventist Health Study 2, EPIC-Oxford); lipid trials | **Strong** for lower LDL and heart disease; higher stroke and fracture risk seen in EPIC-Oxford needs confirmation |
| Low-carbohydrate | Carbohydrate below about 26% of energy | Weight and glycaemic trials | **Strong** for short-term glycaemic control; long-term equivalence for weight |
| Ketogenic | Carbohydrate below about 20–50 g/day | Epilepsy RCTs | **Established** for drug-resistant epilepsy |
| Carnivore | Animal foods only | None of quality | **Not supported** |
| Raw food | Uncooked foods only | Small studies | **Not supported**; cooking improves digestibility and food safety |
| Paleo | "Pre-agricultural" foods | Small, short trials | **Uncertain**; real Palaeolithic diets varied enormously |

## The shared core

Every pattern with good outcome evidence emphasises minimally processed plants and limits processed meat,
sugary drinks and refined starches. Arguments over the margins — olive oil versus seed oil, dairy or no dairy,
fish or no fish — matter much less than this core.

## Sources

- Estruch R et al. Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease with a Mediterranean diet supplemented with extra-virgin olive oil or nuts (PREDIMED, republished). *NEJM* 2018. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1800389](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1800389)
- Appel LJ et al. A clinical trial of the effects of dietary patterns on blood pressure (DASH). *NEJM* 1997. [doi:10.1056/NEJM199704173361601](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199704173361601)
- Delgado-Lista J et al. Long-term secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease with a Mediterranean diet and a low-fat diet (CORDIOPREV). *Lancet* 2022.
- Melina V et al. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: vegetarian diets. *J Acad Nutr Diet* 2016.
- Tong TYN et al. Risks of ischaemic heart disease and stroke in meat eaters, fish eaters, and vegetarians (EPIC-Oxford). *BMJ* 2019.
- Martin-McGill KJ et al. Ketogenic diets for drug-resistant epilepsy. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2020.
- Newman SJ. Supercentenarian and remarkable age records exhibit patterns indicative of clerical errors and pension fraud. *bioRxiv* 2019 (preprint).

title: Meat, dairy and eggs
questions:
  - id: iarc-meat

  - id: processed-def
    prompt: Which foods count as processed meat in the IARC definition?
    type: multiple

        correct: true
      - text: Sausages and hot dogs
        correct: true
      - text: Salami and corned beef
        correct: true
      - text: A fresh, unseasoned chicken breast

        correct: true
      - text: It found meat prevents cancer
      - text: It was based on a 50-year RCT
    explanation: The authors largely agreed on the size of the associations; they disagreed about how certain they were and how much small risks matter to individuals. This is a genuine scientific dispute about evidence standards.
  - id: eggs

    options:

        correct: true
      - text: Eggs are proven to prevent heart disease

      - text: Most of the world's adults lose some ability to digest lactose

## Learning objectives

- Interpret the IARC meat classifications
- Understand why scientists disagree about meat recommendations
- Weigh evidence on eggs and dairy

## Meat

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Processed meat increases colorectal cancer risk | **Strong** to **Established** (IARC Group 1) |
| Red meat increases colorectal cancer risk | **Strong** (IARC 2A, "probably") |
| Processed meat is associated with higher heart disease and diabetes risk | **Strong** (observational, consistent) |
| Unprocessed red meat increases heart disease risk | **Uncertain** to **Strong** — associations are weaker and more variable |
| The absolute risk increase is small for any one person | **Established** — but it applies across hundreds of millions of people |
| Meat is necessary for health | **Not supported** — well-planned vegetarian diets are adequate |
| Lean meat provides high-quality protein, iron, zinc and B12 | **Established** |

The World Cancer Research Fund recommends eating little, if any, processed meat and no more than about
350–500 g (cooked) of red meat per week.

## Dairy

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Dairy is a good source of calcium, protein, iodine, B12 | **Established** |
| Dairy probably lowers colorectal cancer risk | **Strong** (WCRF "probable") |
| Fermented dairy (yoghurt) is associated with lower type 2 diabetes risk | **Uncertain** to **Strong** |
| Full-fat dairy is healthier than low-fat | **Uncertain** — cohort data do not show clear harm from full-fat cheese and yoghurt; butter raises LDL |
| Milk causes mucus production | **Not supported** — trials found no increase in measured mucus |
| Raw milk is healthier than pasteurised | **Not supported** (see the food-safety chapter) |

## Eggs

One large egg contains about 186 mg cholesterol, 6 g protein and useful choline, lutein and vitamin D.
Grade for moderate egg intake causing heart disease in healthy people: **Uncertain**.

## Sources

- Bouvard V et al. Carcinogenicity of consumption of red and processed meat. *Lancet Oncol* 2015. [doi:10.1016/S1470-2045(15)00444-1](https://doi.org/10.1016/S1470-2045(15)00444-1)
- Johnston BC et al. Unprocessed red meat and processed meat consumption: dietary guideline recommendations from the NutriRECS Consortium. *Ann Intern Med* 2019.
- World Cancer Research Fund / AICR. Continuous Update Project, Third Expert Report. 2018.
- Zhong VW et al. Associations of dietary cholesterol or egg consumption with incident cardiovascular disease and mortality. *JAMA* 2019.
- Drouin-Chartier JP et al. Egg consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease: three large prospective US cohort studies and updated meta-analysis. *BMJ* 2020.
- Storhaug CL et al. Country, regional, and global estimates for lactose malabsorption in adults. *Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol* 2017.

      - text: Yes, dramatically
      - id: no-effect
        text: No — clinical-trial meta-analyses found no meaningful effect on testosterone or oestrogen levels at typical intakes
        correct: true
    explanation: Case reports involve extreme intakes. The claim is **Not supported**.
  - id: nuts
    prompt: Which statement about nuts is best supported?
    options:
      - id: lower-cvd
        text: Regular nut consumption is associated with lower cardiovascular disease, and nut-supplemented diets reduced events in PREDIMED
        correct: true
      - text: Nuts cause weight gain so should be avoided
      - text: Nuts contain no fat
    explanation: Despite their energy density, nuts are not linked to weight gain in trials, partly because some fat is not absorbed and they are satiating.
  - id: legumes
    prompt: Which are benefits of legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas, peas)?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: High in fibre and protein
        correct: true
      - text: Lower LDL cholesterol in trials
        correct: true
      - text: Rich in folate, potassium and iron
        correct: true
      - text: High in saturated fat
    explanation: Lectins in raw kidney beans are genuinely toxic, but proper soaking and boiling destroys them. Lectin-avoidance diets based on that fact are **Not supported** for cooked legumes.
  - id: lectins
    prompt: Why must dried red kidney beans be boiled properly, not just slow-cooked at low temperature?
    options:
      - text: To improve flavour only
      - id: pha
        text: They contain phytohaemagglutinin, a lectin that causes severe vomiting if not destroyed by vigorous boiling
        correct: true
      - text: They are radioactive
    explanation: Undercooked beans in slow cookers have caused outbreaks. Canned beans are already cooked.
  - id: superfood
    prompt: What is the scientific meaning of the term "superfood"?
    options:
      - text: A food certified by the WHO
      - id: marketing
        text: None — it is a marketing term with no regulatory or scientific definition
        correct: true
      - text: A food with more than 10 vitamins
    explanation: The EU has restricted the use of "superfood" on labels unless it is accompanied by an authorised health claim. Kale and blueberries are good foods; they are not magic.
  - id: juice
    prompt: How does fruit juice compare with whole fruit?
    options:
      - id: worse
        text: Juice loses most fibre and is easy to over-consume; whole fruit is associated with lower type 2 diabetes risk while juice is not
        correct: true
      - text: Juice is identical to whole fruit
      - text: Juice contains more fibre than fruit
    explanation: This is why WHO counts sugars in juice as free sugars.
---
## Learning objectives

- Quantify the evidence for fruit and vegetables
- Address common fears about soy and lectins
- Recognise "superfood" marketing

## Evidence summary

| Food group | Main associations | Grade |
|-----------|------------------|-------|
| Vegetables and fruit | Lower cardiovascular disease and mortality | **Strong** |
| Whole grains | Lower heart disease, type 2 diabetes, colorectal cancer | **Strong** |
| Legumes | Lower LDL; associated with lower heart disease | **Strong** for LDL; cohort data moderate |
| Nuts | Lower cardiovascular disease | **Strong** |
| Soy foods | Lower LDL modestly; neutral or protective for breast cancer | **Strong** |
| Potatoes | Neutral when boiled or baked; fried potatoes associated with harm | **Uncertain** |
| Fruit juice | Neutral to modestly adverse | **Uncertain** |

## Fears that are not supported

- **Lectins and "anti-nutrients":** phytates and oxalates reduce some mineral absorption, but whole-food
  diets rich in legumes and grains are associated with better health. Cooking, soaking and fermenting reduce
  them. Those prone to calcium-oxalate kidney stones may need medical advice on oxalate
- **Nightshades and inflammation:** no good evidence that tomatoes, peppers or aubergines cause inflammation in
  people without a specific allergy
- **Fruit sugar:** whole fruit is not linked to obesity or diabetes

## Sources

- Aune D et al. Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality. *Int J Epidemiol* 2017.
- Reed KE et al. Neither soy nor isoflavone intake affects male reproductive hormones: an expanded and updated meta-analysis. *Reprod Toxicol* 2021.
- Nachvak SM et al. Soy, soy isoflavones, and protein intake in relation to mortality from all causes, cancers, and cardiovascular diseases. *J Acad Nutr Diet* 2019.
- Aune D et al. Nut consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer, all-cause and cause-specific mortality. *BMC Med* 2016.
- Muraki I et al. Fruit consumption and risk of type 2 diabetes. *BMJ* 2013.

title: Ultra-processed foods
questions:
  - id: nova
    prompt: In the NOVA classification, what defines an ultra-processed food?
    options:
      - text: Any food that has been cooked
      - id: industrial
        text: Industrial formulations made mostly from substances extracted or derived from foods, often with additives such as emulsifiers, flavourings and colours not used in home cooking
        correct: true
      - text: Any food sold in a package
    explanation: Frozen vegetables, plain yoghurt and canned beans are processed but not ultra-processed. Soft drinks, packaged snacks, instant noodles and many breakfast cereals are ultra-processed.
  - id: hall-2019
    prompt: In Kevin Hall's 2019 metabolic-ward trial, how much more did people eat on an ultra-processed diet than on a minimally processed one, when both were matched for presented calories, sugar, fat, fibre and sodium?
    options:
      - text: About 50 kcal/day
      - id: five-hundred
        text: About 500 kcal/day, gaining about 0.9 kg in two weeks
        correct: true
      - text: About 3,000 kcal/day
    explanation: The participants ate faster on the ultra-processed diet. It was a small (20 people), short trial, but it is the strongest causal evidence available. Larger follow-up trials are under way.
  - id: limits
    prompt: Which are genuine criticisms of the NOVA and ultra-processed food concept?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Experts classifying the same foods often disagree
        correct: true
      - text: The category lumps together very different products, such as wholegrain packaged bread and sugary soft drinks
        correct: true
      - text: Most evidence is observational and may be confounded by income and lifestyle
        correct: true
      - text: There is no data on ultra-processed foods at all
    explanation: These criticisms are why the grade is **Strong** for association and only **Uncertain-to-Strong** for causation, and why the mechanism (energy density, palatability, speed of eating, additives) is still debated.
  - id: umbrella
    prompt: A 2024 BMJ umbrella review linked higher ultra-processed food intake with which outcomes?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Cardiovascular disease death
        correct: true
      - text: Type 2 diabetes
        correct: true
      - text: Common mental-health disorders
        correct: true
      - text: Increased lifespan
    explanation: The review graded evidence for some associations as convincing and for others as weak. All were associations.
  - id: processed-not-bad
    prompt: Which of these processed foods are associated with good health or are nutritionally valuable?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Frozen vegetables
        correct: true
      - text: Canned beans and fish
        correct: true
      - text: Pasteurised milk and plain yoghurt
        correct: true
      - text: Fortified wholegrain cereals with little sugar
        correct: true
    explanation: Processing per se is not the problem. Pasteurisation, freezing, canning, fortification and fermentation have prevented enormous disease.
  - id: dga-upf
    prompt: How did the 2025–2030 US Dietary Guidelines treat processed foods?
    options:
      - id: limit
        text: They urged limiting highly processed foods, sugar-sweetened beverages and refined carbohydrates
        correct: true
      - text: They recommended eating mostly ultra-processed foods
      - text: They did not mention processing
    explanation: This was one of the more evidence-aligned changes, though a formal definition of "highly processed" was not established.
---
## Learning objectives

- Define ultra-processed food
- Assess the evidence and its limits
- Separate processing from nutrition

## The NOVA groups

| Group | Description | Examples |
|-------|-------------|----------|
| 1 | Unprocessed or minimally processed | Fresh fruit, eggs, milk, frozen vegetables, plain nuts |
| 2 | Processed culinary ingredients | Oils, butter, sugar, salt |
| 3 | Processed foods | Canned vegetables, cheese, freshly made bread, cured meats |
| 4 | Ultra-processed foods | Soft drinks, packaged snacks, sweetened cereals, reconstituted meat products, instant noodles |

In the US and UK, ultra-processed foods provide over half of energy intake.

## What is known

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| High UPF intake is associated with obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and mortality | **Strong** (association) |
| Ultra-processed diets can cause overeating | **Strong** but rests mainly on one small ward trial |
| The harms are fully explained by sugar, fat, salt and low fibre | **Uncertain** |
| Specific additives (some emulsifiers, for example) harm gut health in humans | **Uncertain** — animal and early human data |
| All processing is harmful | **Not supported** |

## Practical meaning

Diets built around minimally processed foods tend to be higher in fibre and lower in energy density, sugar and
salt. That remains good advice whatever the final explanation turns out to be.

## Sources

- Hall KD et al. Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain: an inpatient randomized controlled trial of ad libitum food intake. *Cell Metab* 2019. [doi:10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008)
- Monteiro CA et al. Ultra-processed foods: what they are and how to identify them. *Public Health Nutr* 2019.
- Lane MM et al. Ultra-processed food exposure and adverse health outcomes: umbrella review of epidemiological meta-analyses. *BMJ* 2024.
- Braesco V et al. Ultra-processed foods: how functional is the NOVA system? *Eur J Clin Nutr* 2022.

title: Heart disease and stroke
questions:
  - id: risk-factors
    prompt: Which are diet-related, causal risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: High LDL cholesterol
        correct: true
      - text: High blood pressure
        correct: true
      - text: Type 2 diabetes
        correct: true
      - text: Obesity
        correct: true
      - text: Eating food after 8 pm
    explanation: Smoking, physical inactivity and genetics such as familial hypercholesterolaemia and lipoprotein(a) are also major risk factors.
  - id: gbd-diet
    prompt: The Global Burden of Disease 2017 diet analysis estimated that poor diet was responsible for about how many deaths worldwide in one year?
    options:
      - text: About 100,000
      - id: eleven-million
        text: About 11 million
        correct: true
      - text: About 500 million
    explanation: The leading dietary risks were high sodium, low whole grains and low fruit. These are modelled estimates with large uncertainty, but the order of magnitude is consistent across analyses.
  - id: ldl-causal
    prompt: Which kinds of evidence together establish LDL cholesterol as a cause of atherosclerosis?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Genetic studies (familial hypercholesterolaemia; Mendelian randomisation)
        correct: true
      - text: Prospective cohort studies
        correct: true
      - text: RCTs of LDL-lowering drugs reducing events in proportion to LDL lowering
        correct: true
      - text: Testimonials from people who feel healthy with high LDL
    explanation: The 2017 European Atherosclerosis Society consensus summarised over 200 studies with more than 2 million participants. The "LDL doesn't matter" claim is **Not supported**.
  - id: portfolio
    prompt: The "portfolio diet" combines plant sterols, viscous fibre, soy protein and nuts. In controlled trials, how much did it lower LDL?
    options:
      - text: Not at all
      - id: like-statin
        text: Around 20–30% in some feeding trials — comparable to a low-dose statin — though less in free-living conditions
        correct: true
      - text: It raised LDL
    explanation: Diet can lower LDL meaningfully. People with very high LDL or established disease usually still need medication; diet and drugs are complementary, not competing.
  - id: lyon
    prompt: The Lyon Diet Heart Study tested a Mediterranean-style diet after a first heart attack. What happened?
    options:
      - id: large-reduction
        text: It found a large reduction in recurrent cardiac events and deaths, although the trial was small and had methodological limitations
        correct: true
      - text: The diet increased heart attacks
      - text: No one was followed up
    explanation: Combined with PREDIMED and CORDIOPREV, the Mediterranean pattern has unusually good trial support for a dietary pattern.
  - id: chelation
    prompt: What is the grade for using "detox" diets or chelation therapy to "clean out" arteries?
    options:
      - text: Established
      - id: not-supported
        text: Not supported
        correct: true
      - text: Strong
    explanation: Arteries are not pipes that can be flushed with juice. Chelation therapy has caused deaths; the TACT trial's modest results were debated and did not change guidelines for the general public.
  - id: salt-bp
    prompt: Who tends to show the largest blood-pressure fall when they reduce salt?
    options:
      - id: hypertensive
        text: People with high blood pressure, older adults and, on average, Black adults
        correct: true
      - text: Only young athletes
      - text: Nobody — salt does not affect blood pressure
    explanation: Salt sensitivity varies, but average population reductions lower blood pressure and are expected to prevent strokes.
---
## Learning objectives

- Identify dietary contributors to cardiovascular disease
- Understand why LDL causality is established
- Know which dietary interventions have trial support

## What diet changes

| Dietary change | Effect | Grade |
|---------------|--------|-------|
| Replace saturated with unsaturated fat | Lowers LDL and events | **Strong** |
| Eliminate industrial trans fat | Lowers events | **Established** |
| Reduce sodium; increase potassium | Lowers blood pressure and stroke | **Established** (BP), **Strong** (events) |
| Mediterranean pattern | Fewer events in PREDIMED, Lyon, CORDIOPREV | **Strong** |
| More fibre, whole grains, legumes, nuts | Lower LDL and risk | **Strong** |
| Weight loss in obesity | Lowers BP, LDL, glucose | **Established** for risk factors |
| Plant sterols/stanols 2 g/day | Lowers LDL about 10% | **Established** for LDL; outcomes not tested |
| Fish-oil supplements in healthy people | No event reduction | **Not supported** |
| Antioxidant supplements | No event reduction | **Not supported** |
| Garlic pills, turmeric, apple cider vinegar | Small or no effects on risk factors | **Uncertain** to **Not supported** |

## The role of medicine

Statins, PCSK9 inhibitors, ezetimibe, blood-pressure drugs and GLP-1 agonists reduce events in RCTs.
Diet is foundational, and it is not a substitute for medication when medication is indicated. Advising
people to stop proven drugs in favour of diet alone is dangerous.

## Sources

- GBD 2017 Diet Collaborators. Health effects of dietary risks in 195 countries. *Lancet* 2019. [doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(19)30041-8](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(19)30041-8)
- Ference BA et al. Low-density lipoproteins cause atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. *Eur Heart J* 2017. [doi:10.1093/eurheartj/ehx144](https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehx144)
- Jenkins DJA et al. Effect of a dietary portfolio of cholesterol-lowering foods vs lovastatin. *JAMA* 2003.
- de Lorgeril M et al. Mediterranean diet, traditional risk factors, and the rate of cardiovascular complications after myocardial infarction (Lyon Diet Heart Study). *Circulation* 1999.
- Arnett DK et al. 2019 ACC/AHA guideline on the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease. *Circulation* 2019.

      - text: 5%

        correct: true
      - text: 100%

  - id: direct
    prompt: What did the DiRECT trial in UK primary care show?
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: Diet has no effect on type 2 diabetes
      - text: Type 2 diabetes was cured permanently in everyone
    explanation: Remission (normal glucose without medication) declined over five years as weight was regained, but remained much higher than control. Remission is most likely early in the disease.
  - id: type1
    prompt: Can diet cure type 1 diabetes?
    options:
      - text: Yes, with a raw vegan diet
      - text: Yes, with cinnamon
      - id: no-cure
        text: No — type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing cells; people with it require insulin, and stopping insulin can be fatal
        correct: true

  - id: sugar-cause

    options:

      - id: indirect

        correct: true
      - text: Sugar prevents diabetes

  - id: cinnamon

    options:
      - text: Established — they can replace medication
      - id: uncertain-small

        correct: true
    explanation: Cassia cinnamon in large amounts contains coumarin, which can harm the liver.
  - id: risk-foods

    type: multiple

        correct: true
      - text: Coffee
        correct: true
      - text: Yoghurt
        correct: true
      - text: Processed meat
      - text: Sugar-sweetened beverages
    explanation: Processed meat and sugary drinks are associated with higher risk. All of these are cohort associations of varying strength.
  - id: look-ahead
    prompt: The Look AHEAD trial of intensive lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes was stopped for futility. Why?
    options:
      - id: no-cv

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish type 1 and type 2 diabetes
- Know the prevention and remission trials
- Recognise unsupported "cures"

## Prevention and remission

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Lifestyle intervention prevents or delays type 2 diabetes in high-risk adults | **Established** |
| Substantial weight loss can put early type 2 diabetes into remission | **Established** (DiRECT, bariatric surgery) |
| GLP-1 drugs and tirzepatide lower glucose and weight markedly | **Established** |
| Low-carbohydrate diets lower HbA1c in the short term | **Strong** |
| Any specific spice or supplement cures diabetes | **Not supported** |
| Diet can replace insulin in type 1 diabetes | **Not supported** — and dangerous |

## Sources

- Knowler WC et al. Reduction in the incidence of type 2 diabetes with lifestyle intervention or metformin (DPP). *NEJM* 2002. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa012512](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa012512)

- Look AHEAD Research Group. Cardiovascular effects of intensive lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes. *NEJM* 2013. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1212914](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1212914)
- Tuomilehto J et al. Prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus by changes in lifestyle (Finnish DPS). *NEJM* 2001.
- American Diabetes Association. Standards of Care in Diabetes. Updated annually.

## Learning objectives

- Rank dietary factors in cancer by strength of evidence
- Reject cancer-cure diets
- Understand why single-food claims mislead

## Estimated scale

In the UK, Cancer Research UK estimates about 4 in 10 cancer cases are preventable, with smoking first and
excess weight second. Alcohol, low fibre and processed meat each contribute a few percent.

## Evidence summary (WCRF/AICR and IARC)

| Exposure | Cancer | Grade |
|----------|--------|-------|
| Alcohol | Mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, breast, colorectum | **Established** |
| Excess body fat | 13+ sites | **Established** |
| Processed meat | Colorectal | **Established** (Group 1) |
| Red meat | Colorectal | **Strong** (probable) |
| Aflatoxins | Liver | **Established** |
| Salt-preserved foods | Stomach | **Strong** |
| Whole grains, fibre | Colorectal (protective) | **Strong** (probable) |
| Dairy and calcium | Colorectal (protective) | **Strong** (probable) |
| Physical activity | Colon, breast, endometrium (protective) | **Established** to **Strong** |
| Very hot drinks above 65 °C | Oesophagus | **Strong** (IARC 2A) |
| Sugar "feeds" cancer | — | **Not supported** as a direct mechanism |
| Alkaline diet, juice fasts, apricot kernels (laetrile), coffee enemas | Cure | **Not supported**; laetrile can cause cyanide poisoning |

## Sources

- World Cancer Research Fund / AICR. *Diet, Nutrition, Physical Activity and Cancer: a Global Perspective.* Third Expert Report, 2018.
- Lauby-Secretan B et al. Body fatness and cancer — viewpoint of the IARC Working Group. *NEJM* 2016.
- Johnson SB et al. Use of alternative medicine for cancer and its impact on survival. *J Natl Cancer Inst* 2018.
- Nelson KM et al. The essential medicinal chemistry of curcumin. *J Med Chem* 2017.

title: The gut microbiome
questions:
  - id: established-microbiome
    prompt: Which microbiome-based treatment is **Established** by RCTs?
    options:
      - id: fmt
        text: Faecal microbiota transplantation for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection
        correct: true
      - text: Probiotics to cure autism
      - text: Kombucha to cure depression
    explanation: FMT cures a large majority of recurrent C. difficile infections — the clearest proof that the gut microbiome matters. Most other microbiome claims are early-stage.
  - id: probiotics-aad
    prompt: For which use do probiotics have the most consistent evidence?
    options:
      - id: aad
        text: Reducing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (moderate certainty)
        correct: true
      - text: Weight loss in healthy adults
      - text: Preventing all infections
    explanation: Effects depend on the strain and dose; "probiotic" is not one thing. A 2018 study found that probiotics after antibiotics delayed the return of a person's normal microbiome compared with no treatment.
  - id: association
    prompt: Many studies show people with a disease have a different microbiome. What is the key limitation?
    options:
      - id: direction
        text: Differences may be a consequence of the disease, its treatment or diet, rather than a cause
        correct: true
      - text: The microbiome cannot be measured
      - text: Bacteria do not live in the gut
    explanation: Reverse causation applies here too. Causality requires interventions that change the microbiome and then change the outcome.
  - id: fibre-feeds
    prompt: What do gut bacteria produce when they ferment dietary fibre?
    options:
      - id: scfa
        text: Short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate, acetate and propionate
        correct: true
      - text: Vitamin C
      - text: Ethanol in dangerous amounts in everyone
    explanation: Butyrate is the main fuel for colon cells. This is one plausible mechanism for fibre's benefits.
  - id: tests
    prompt: What is the evidence grade for direct-to-consumer microbiome tests that recommend personalised diets?
    options:
      - text: Established
      - id: uncertain
        text: Uncertain at best — there is no agreed definition of a "healthy" microbiome, and test results vary between companies
        correct: true
      - text: Strong
    explanation: Research on personalised glucose responses (for example the Weizmann and PREDICT studies) is interesting, but consumer tests are ahead of the evidence.
  - id: leaky-gut
    prompt: Which statement about "leaky gut syndrome" is accurate?
    options:
      - text: It is a well-defined disease with a standard diagnostic test
      - id: not-diagnosis
        text: Increased intestinal permeability is a real, measurable phenomenon in some diseases, but "leaky gut syndrome" as a cause of a wide range of symptoms is not an established diagnosis
        correct: true
      - text: Intestinal permeability does not exist
    explanation: Products sold to "heal the leaky gut" generally lack trial evidence.
  - id: fermented
    prompt: In a 2021 Stanford trial, a diet high in fermented foods for 10 weeks compared with a high-fibre diet did what?
    options:
      - id: diversity
        text: Increased microbiome diversity and reduced several inflammatory markers
        correct: true
      - text: Caused weight gain of 10 kg
      - text: Had no measurable effect on anything
    explanation: It was a small (36 people) study. Interesting and plausible, but clinical outcomes were not measured. Grade - **Uncertain**.
---
## Learning objectives

- Separate established microbiome science from hype
- Understand the limitations of association studies
- Evaluate probiotic claims

## What is known

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids | **Established** |
| FMT cures recurrent C. difficile infection | **Established** |
| Antibiotics disrupt the microbiome | **Established** |
| Probiotics reduce antibiotic-associated diarrhoea | **Strong** (strain-dependent) |
| Microbiome differences cause obesity in humans | **Uncertain** |
| Fermented foods improve health outcomes | **Uncertain** |
| Probiotic supplements benefit healthy people | **Uncertain** |
| Consumer microbiome tests guide better diets | **Uncertain** to **Not supported** |
| Detox colon cleanses improve the microbiome | **Not supported** |

## Sources

- van Nood E et al. Duodenal infusion of donor feces for recurrent Clostridium difficile. *NEJM* 2013.
- Goldenberg JZ et al. Probiotics for the prevention of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2017.
- Suez J et al. Post-antibiotic gut mucosal microbiome reconstitution is impaired by probiotics and improved by autologous FMT. *Cell* 2018.
- Wastyk HC et al. Gut-microbiota-targeted diets modulate human immune status. *Cell* 2021.
- Zeevi D et al. Personalized nutrition by prediction of glycemic responses. *Cell* 2015.

title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and infancy
questions:
  - id: folic
    prompt: The 1991 MRC Vitamin Study found that folic acid supplementation before conception and in early pregnancy reduced recurrence of neural tube defects by about how much?
    options:
      - text: 5%
      - id: seventy-two
        text: 72%
        correct: true
      - text: 0%
    explanation: Neural tube closure happens around four weeks after conception, often before a pregnancy is known — which is why the advice applies to anyone who could become pregnant. Mandatory fortification of flour has reduced neural tube defects in over 80 countries.
  - id: avoid
    prompt: Which should be avoided during pregnancy?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Alcohol
        correct: true
      - text: Unpasteurised milk and soft cheeses made from it
        correct: true
      - text: High-mercury fish such as shark, swordfish, king mackerel and bigeye tuna
        correct: true
      - text: High-dose preformed vitamin A supplements and large amounts of liver
        correct: true
      - text: All fish
    explanation: Low-mercury fish such as salmon, sardines and cod are recommended 2–3 times weekly for omega-3 and other nutrients. Pregnant women are about 10 times more likely than the general population to get listeriosis (CDC).
  - id: weight-gain
    prompt: Is "eating for two" good advice?
    options:
      - text: Yes, energy needs double
      - id: modest
        text: No — extra energy needs are modest, about 340 kcal/day in the second trimester and 450 kcal/day in the third, with none extra in the first
        correct: true
    explanation: Recommended weight gain depends on pre-pregnancy BMI (US National Academies 2009). Nutrient needs (folate, iron, iodine) rise more than energy needs.
  - id: breastfeeding
    prompt: What does the WHO recommend for infant feeding?
    options:
      - id: exclusive-six
        text: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, then continued breastfeeding with complementary foods up to two years or beyond
        correct: true
      - text: Cow's milk from birth
      - text: Solid food from one month
    explanation: Benefits for infections in infancy are **Established**; some long-term benefits seen in cohorts (IQ, obesity) are smaller in sibling and RCT analyses (PROBIT) and remain **Uncertain** in size. Infant formula is a safe, nutritionally complete alternative when breastfeeding is not possible.
  - id: leap
    prompt: What did the LEAP trial (2015) show about peanut introduction in high-risk infants?
    options:
      - text: Early peanut exposure caused more allergy
      - id: early-reduces
        text: Introducing peanut early (from 4–11 months) reduced peanut allergy by about 81% compared with avoidance
        correct: true
      - text: Peanuts should be avoided until age 10
    explanation: This reversed earlier avoidance advice — a good example of science updating guidance based on an RCT. Guidelines now recommend introducing allergenic foods early.
  - id: honey-infant
    prompt: Why must honey not be given to infants under 12 months?
    options:
      - id: botulism
        text: It can contain Clostridium botulinum spores, which can cause infant botulism
        correct: true
      - text: It causes diabetes
      - text: It contains gluten
    explanation: Older children and adults have mature gut flora that prevent the spores from colonising the gut.
  - id: cows-milk
    prompt: Why is cow's milk not recommended as a main drink before 12 months?
    options:
      - id: iron-kidney
        text: It is low in iron, can cause intestinal blood loss in young infants, and has a high protein and mineral load for immature kidneys
        correct: true
      - text: It is toxic at any age
      - text: Babies cannot taste it
    explanation: Small amounts in cooking are fine after about six months.
  - id: plant-milk-infant
    prompt: Are rice, almond or oat drinks suitable replacements for breast milk or infant formula?
    options:
      - text: Yes, they are healthier
      - id: dangerous
        text: No — they are nutritionally inadequate for infants, and their use has caused severe malnutrition and deaths
        correct: true
    explanation: Rice drinks are also not recommended for children under about five years in the UK because of arsenic content.
---
## Learning objectives

- Know the critical nutrients and hazards in pregnancy
- Understand infant feeding evidence
- Recognise how early-allergen guidance changed

## Pregnancy essentials

| Nutrient or practice | Recommendation | Grade |
|----------------------|----------------|-------|
| Folic acid | 400 µg/day from before conception through week 12 (higher doses for some) | **Established** |
| Iodine | 220 µg/day; many guidelines suggest a 150 µg supplement | **Strong** |
| Iron | 27 mg/day RDA; supplement if deficient | **Established** |
| Vitamin D | 10 µg (400 IU) daily in UK guidance | **Strong** |
| Alcohol | None | **Established** (harm), precautionary (low dose) |
| Caffeine | Below 200 mg/day | **Strong** |
| Low-mercury fish | 2–3 servings/week | **Strong** |
| Listeria-risk foods | Avoid unpasteurised dairy, deli meats unless reheated, refrigerated smoked fish | **Established** |

## Infancy

- Vitamin K injection at birth — **Established**
- Vitamin D 400 IU/day for breastfed infants — **Established**
- Solid foods around six months, not before four — **Strong**
- Early introduction of peanut and egg — **Established** for peanut in high-risk infants (LEAP)
- No honey before 12 months — **Established**
- No added salt or sugar — **Strong**

## Sources

- MRC Vitamin Study Research Group. Prevention of neural tube defects: results of the Medical Research Council Vitamin Study. *Lancet* 1991.
- Du Toit G et al. Randomized trial of peanut consumption in infants at risk for peanut allergy (LEAP). *NEJM* 2015. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1414850](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1414850)
- Kramer MS et al. Promotion of Breastfeeding Intervention Trial (PROBIT). *JAMA* 2001; *Arch Gen Psychiatry* 2008.
- Institute of Medicine. *Weight Gain During Pregnancy: Reexamining the Guidelines.* 2009.
- US FDA and EPA. Advice about eating fish. Updated 2022.
- WHO. Infant and young child feeding fact sheet.

title: Children, adolescents and older adults
questions:
  - id: stunting
    prompt: What is stunting?
    options:
      - id: low-height
        text: Low height for age caused by chronic undernutrition and repeated infection, especially in the first 1,000 days
        correct: true
      - text: Normal variation in height
      - text: A result of drinking coffee
    explanation: WHO and UNICEF estimate about 150 million children under five are stunted, with lasting effects on health and cognition.
  - id: double-burden
    prompt: What does the "double burden of malnutrition" refer to?
    options:
      - id: both
        text: Undernutrition and obesity coexisting in the same country, community or even household
        correct: true
      - text: Eating two dinners
      - text: Being deficient in two vitamins
    explanation: Many low- and middle-income countries now face both problems simultaneously.
  - id: picky
    prompt: How many times might a child need to be offered a new food before accepting it, according to feeding research?
    options:
      - text: Once
      - id: many
        text: Often 8–15 times
        correct: true
      - text: Never — preferences are fixed at birth
    explanation: Repeated, pressure-free exposure works better than forcing, bribing or rewarding with sweets.
  - id: sarcopenia
    prompt: Which combination best slows sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss)?
    options:
      - id: resistance-protein
        text: Resistance exercise combined with adequate protein
        correct: true
      - text: Collagen supplements alone
      - text: Bed rest
    explanation: Resistance training is the main driver; protein supports it. Supplements alone produce little benefit in people already eating enough.
  - id: older-risks
    prompt: Which nutritional problems are more common in older adults?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Vitamin B12 deficiency due to reduced stomach acid
        correct: true
      - text: Dehydration due to blunted thirst
        correct: true
      - text: Unintentional weight loss and undernutrition, especially in care homes
        correct: true
      - text: Scurvy from eating too many oranges
    explanation: In older adults, unintended weight loss is often more dangerous than modest excess weight; screening tools such as MUST help detect malnutrition.
  - id: obesity-paradox
    prompt: In older adults, a BMI in the "overweight" range is sometimes associated with lower mortality than "normal" BMI. What is a likely explanation?
    options:
      - id: confounding
        text: Reverse causation (illness causes weight loss) and poor measurement of body composition, though the true optimum BMI may shift somewhat upward with age
        correct: true
      - text: Fat is protective at every age
      - text: BMI cannot be measured in older people
    explanation: This "obesity paradox" is a genuine research debate. Grade for the optimal BMI in older adults - **Uncertain**.
  - id: school-meals
    prompt: What does evidence suggest about school meal and sugary-drink policies?
    options:
      - id: modest
        text: Healthier school food standards and sugar-drink taxes produce measurable, modest improvements in intake, with mixed evidence on obesity rates
        correct: true
      - text: They have been proven to eliminate childhood obesity
      - text: They have never been evaluated
    explanation: The UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy (2018) led manufacturers to reformulate, cutting sugar in drinks substantially. Health effects are still being evaluated.
---
## Learning objectives

- Know nutrition priorities in childhood and old age
- Understand undernutrition as well as overnutrition

## Children

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| The first 1,000 days (conception to age two) are critical for growth and brain development | **Established** |
| Repeated exposure increases acceptance of vegetables | **Strong** |
| Sugary drinks contribute to excess weight and tooth decay in children | **Strong** to **Established** |
| Fruit juice should be limited (AAP — none under 12 months; up to 120 ml for ages 1–3) | **Strong** |
| Sugar causes hyperactivity | **Not supported** |
| Children need special "toddler milks" | **Not supported** — these are unnecessary per WHO and AAP |

## Older adults

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Protein needs are higher (about 1.0–1.2 g/kg) | **Strong** |
| B12 deficiency is common and under-diagnosed | **Strong** |
| Vitamin D plus calcium reduces fractures in institutionalised elderly | **Strong** |
| Antioxidant supplements prevent dementia | **Not supported** |
| The MIND diet prevents dementia | **Uncertain** — a 2023 RCT found no significant cognitive benefit over a control diet with mild calorie restriction |

## Sources

- Victora CG et al. Revisiting maternal and child undernutrition in low-income and middle-income countries. *Lancet* 2021.
- UNICEF/WHO/World Bank. Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates. 2023.
- Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al. Sarcopenia: revised European consensus. *Age Ageing* 2019.
- Barnes LL et al. Trial of the MIND diet for prevention of cognitive decline in older persons. *NEJM* 2023.
- Rogers NT et al. Associations between trajectories of obesity prevalence in English primary school children and the UK soft drinks industry levy. *PLoS Med* 2023.

title: Sports nutrition
questions:
  - id: ioc-supps
    prompt: Which supplements does the 2018 IOC consensus statement list as having good evidence of performance benefit in some situations?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Caffeine
        correct: true
      - text: Creatine monohydrate
        correct: true
      - text: Nitrate (beetroot juice)
        correct: true
      - text: Beta-alanine
        correct: true
      - text: Sodium bicarbonate
        correct: true
      - text: BCAAs for muscle growth when protein intake is adequate
    explanation: Branched-chain amino acids add nothing when total protein is adequate. Even the good supplements work only in specific sports and conditions.
  - id: creatine
    prompt: What is a typical maintenance dose of creatine monohydrate?
    options:
      - id: three-five
        text: 3–5 g per day
        correct: true
      - text: 100 g per day
      - text: 0.01 g per day
    explanation: Creatine is one of the most-studied supplements; it reliably improves high-intensity, repeated efforts and strength gains. Initial weight gain is mostly water in muscle. It has not been shown to harm healthy kidneys.
  - id: carbs-endurance
    prompt: For endurance events lasting over about 2.5 hours, current guidance suggests carbohydrate intake during exercise of up to about how much?
    options:
      - text: 0 g per hour
      - id: ninety
        text: About 90 g per hour, using mixed glucose and fructose sources
        correct: true
      - text: 500 g per hour
    explanation: Multiple transportable carbohydrates allow higher absorption. Gut training improves tolerance.
  - id: red-s
    prompt: What is Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs)?
    options:
      - id: low-availability
        text: A syndrome caused by low energy availability that impairs hormonal, bone, metabolic and immune health and performance, in athletes of all sexes
        correct: true
      - text: A condition caused by eating too much protein
      - text: A disease only of sprinters
    explanation: It extends the older "female athlete triad" concept. Stress fractures and menstrual dysfunction are warning signs.
  - id: timing
    prompt: How important is the "anabolic window" (consuming protein within 30 minutes of training)?
    options:
      - text: Critical — miss it and training is wasted
      - id: less
        text: Much less important than total daily protein; spreading protein across meals is sensible
        correct: true
    explanation: Meta-analyses found that apparent timing effects mostly disappear once total protein intake is matched.
  - id: ketones-perf
    prompt: What is the evidence grade for ketogenic diets improving high-intensity endurance performance?
    options:
      - text: Established
      - id: not-supported
        text: Not supported — ketogenic adaptation increases fat oxidation but impaired performance at race intensities in elite race walkers
        correct: true
      - text: Strong
    explanation: Burke and colleagues (2017) found that keto-adapted race walkers lost the ability to perform efficiently at high intensity.
  - id: contamination
    prompt: Why do anti-doping agencies warn athletes about supplements?
    options:
      - id: contaminated
        text: Some supplements are contaminated with prohibited substances not listed on the label, and athletes are strictly liable
        correct: true
      - text: Supplements are always illegal
      - text: There is no risk
    explanation: Batch-tested certification programmes reduce, but cannot eliminate, the risk.
---
## Learning objectives

- Set protein and carbohydrate targets for athletes
- Identify the few supplements with good evidence
- Recognise low energy availability

## Targets

| Need | Guidance | Grade |
|------|---------|-------|
| Protein | 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day, about 0.3 g/kg per meal | **Strong** |
| Carbohydrate (daily) | 3–5 g/kg light training; 6–10 g/kg heavy; 8–12 g/kg very heavy endurance | **Strong** |
| Carbohydrate during long events | 30–90 g/hour depending on duration | **Strong** |
| Fluid | Drink to thirst; avoid weight gain during events | **Strong** |

## Supplements with evidence

| Supplement | Benefit | Grade |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| Caffeine 3–6 mg/kg | Endurance and some high-intensity performance | **Established** |
| Creatine | Strength, power, repeated sprints | **Established** |
| Nitrate | Endurance in non-elite athletes | **Strong** |
| Beta-alanine | Efforts of 1–10 minutes | **Strong** |
| Sodium bicarbonate | High-intensity efforts; gut side effects | **Strong** |
| BCAAs, glutamine, testosterone "boosters" | None meaningful | **Not supported** |

## Sources

- Maughan RJ et al. IOC consensus statement: dietary supplements and the high-performance athlete. *Br J Sports Med* 2018.
- Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. Nutrition and athletic performance (ACSM/AND/DC joint position). *Med Sci Sports Exerc* 2016.
- Mountjoy M et al. 2023 IOC consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). *Br J Sports Med* 2023.
- Burke LM et al. Low carbohydrate, high fat diet impairs exercise economy and negates the performance benefit from intensified training in elite race walkers. *J Physiol* 2017.
- Schoenfeld BJ et al. The effect of protein timing on muscle strength and hypertrophy: a meta-analysis. *J Int Soc Sports Nutr* 2013.
- Kreider RB et al. ISSN position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation. *J Int Soc Sports Nutr* 2017.
