title: Food safety and foodborne illness
questions:
  - id: burden
    prompt: CDC estimates that foodborne illness in the US causes roughly how many illnesses each year?
    options:
      - text: About 4,800
      - id: forty-eight-million
        text: About 48 million, with about 128,000 hospitalisations and 3,000 deaths
        correct: true
      - text: About 3 billion
    explanation: These are 2011 estimates; WHO estimates about 600 million cases and 420,000 deaths globally each year.
  - id: danger-zone
    prompt: What is the bacterial "danger zone" for food temperature?
    options:
      - id: four-sixty
        text: About 4–60 °C (40–140 °F)
        correct: true
      - text: Below 0 °C
      - text: Above 100 °C only
    explanation: Perishable food should not sit in this range for more than two hours (one hour above 32 °C / 90 °F).
  - id: poultry-temp
    prompt: What internal temperature does USDA recommend for cooking poultry?
    options:
      - text: 50 °C (122 °F)
      - id: seventy-four
        text: 74 °C (165 °F)
        correct: true
      - text: 100 °C (212 °F) for one hour
    explanation: Ground meats should reach 71 °C (160 °F); whole cuts of beef, pork and lamb 63 °C (145 °F) with a three-minute rest. Colour is not a reliable indicator; use a thermometer.
  - id: washing-chicken
    prompt: Should you wash raw chicken before cooking?
    options:
      - text: Yes, it removes bacteria
      - id: no-splash
        text: No — washing does not reliably remove bacteria and splashes them around the kitchen; cooking kills them
        correct: true
    explanation: A 2019 USDA observational study found that a quarter of participants who washed poultry transferred bacteria to a salad they prepared afterwards.
  - id: listeria
    prompt: Which characteristics make Listeria monocytogenes particularly dangerous?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It can grow at refrigerator temperatures
        correct: true
      - text: It can cause miscarriage, stillbirth and newborn infection
        correct: true
      - text: It has a high fatality rate in older and immunocompromised people
        correct: true
      - text: It is killed by refrigeration
    explanation: High-risk foods include unpasteurised dairy, soft cheeses, deli meats, refrigerated smoked fish and pre-cut melon.
  - id: five-second
    prompt: What did Rutgers researchers (Miranda and Schaffner, 2016) find about the "five-second rule"?
    options:
      - text: Food dropped for under five seconds is sterile
      - id: instant
        text: Bacterial transfer can begin in under one second; moisture and surface type matter more than time
        correct: true
      - text: Bacteria never transfer to food
    explanation: Wet foods like watermelon picked up the most bacteria; carpet transferred less than tile or steel.
  - id: botulism-home
    prompt: Which home practice carries a risk of botulism?
    options:
      - id: low-acid-canning
        text: Home-canning low-acid foods (vegetables, meats) without a pressure canner, or storing garlic in oil at room temperature
        correct: true
      - text: Freezing bread
      - text: Boiling water for tea
    explanation: Clostridium botulinum thrives in low-oxygen, low-acid conditions. Its toxin is among the most lethal substances known.
---
## Learning objectives

- Understand the scale of foodborne illness
- Apply the four core food-safety practices
- Identify high-risk foods and groups

## The four rules

| Rule | What it means |
|------|---------------|
| Clean | Wash hands, surfaces and produce (not raw meat) |
| Separate | Keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat foods |
| Cook | Use a thermometer to reach safe internal temperatures |
| Chill | Refrigerate at 4 °C (40 °F) or below within two hours |

## Major pathogens

| Pathogen | Typical sources | Notes |
|----------|-----------------|-------|
| Norovirus | Ill food handlers, shellfish | Most common cause of foodborne illness |
| Salmonella | Poultry, eggs, produce | Leading cause of hospitalisation and death in the US |
| Campylobacter | Undercooked poultry, raw milk | Can trigger Guillain-Barré syndrome |
| Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7) | Undercooked ground beef, raw milk, leafy greens | Haemolytic uraemic syndrome and kidney failure in children |
| Listeria | Deli meats, soft cheese, raw milk | Dangerous in pregnancy |
| Clostridium botulinum | Improper home canning; honey for infants | Paralysis |

## High-risk groups

Pregnant people, infants and young children, adults over 65 and people with weakened immune systems are
at greatest risk. Their food-safety precautions are not optional extras.

## Sources

- Scallan E et al. Foodborne illness acquired in the United States — major pathogens. *Emerg Infect Dis* 2011.
- WHO. Estimates of the global burden of foodborne diseases. 2015.
- USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service. Safe minimum internal temperature chart.
- Miranda RC, Schaffner DW. Longer contact times increase cross-contamination of Enterobacter aerogenes from surfaces to food. *Appl Environ Microbiol* 2016.
- USDA FSIS. Food safety consumer research project: meal preparation experiment related to poultry washing. 2019.

---
title: Raw milk, sacred-animal remedies and the appeal to purity
questions:
  - id: pasteurisation
    prompt: What does standard high-temperature short-time (HTST) pasteurisation of milk involve?
    options:
      - id: seventy-two
        text: Heating to at least 72 °C (161 °F) for 15 seconds, then rapid cooling
        correct: true
      - text: Boiling milk for an hour
      - text: Adding antibiotics
    explanation: Pasteurisation kills the pathogens that historically made milk a major cause of tuberculosis, typhoid, scarlet fever, diphtheria and infant diarrhoea.
  - id: risk-ratio
    prompt: A 2017 analysis by Costard and colleagues estimated how unpasteurised milk compares with pasteurised milk per unit consumed in the US?
    options:
      - text: Equally safe
      - id: eight-forty
        text: About 840 times more illnesses and 45 times more hospitalisations
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk is ten times safer
    explanation: CDC data for 1998–2018 attributed 202 outbreaks to raw milk, with 2,645 illnesses and 228 hospitalisations, despite only a small fraction of people drinking it. Children are disproportionately affected.
  - id: raw-claims
    prompt: Which common claims about raw milk are **Not supported**?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Pasteurisation destroys milk's nutritional value
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk cures lactose intolerance
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk's "good bacteria" make it safe
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk boosts immunity in a way that outweighs its infection risk
        correct: true
    explanation: Pasteurisation causes only small losses of some heat-sensitive vitamins of which milk is not a major source. A 2014 Stanford randomised crossover trial found raw milk did not reduce lactose malabsorption or symptoms. Pathogens are not neutralised by other bacteria.
  - id: h5n1
    prompt: What happened with H5N1 avian influenza and raw milk in 2024?
    options:
      - text: Nothing — H5N1 cannot infect cattle
      - id: detected
        text: H5N1 spread in US dairy cattle, high virus levels were found in raw milk, farm cats died after drinking it, and raw-milk products were recalled; pasteurisation inactivates the virus
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk was shown to cure H5N1
    explanation: CDC and FDA advise against raw milk, citing H5N1 among other risks. Retail testing of pasteurised milk found viral fragments but no infectious virus.
  - id: farm-asthma
    prompt: European studies (such as GABRIELA) found children on farms who drank farm milk had less asthma and allergy. What is the correct interpretation?
    options:
      - text: Proof that everyone should drink raw milk
      - id: association
        text: An association that may reflect the wider farm environment; the protective component has not been identified, and the infection risk is real — researchers have explicitly not recommended raw milk
        correct: true
      - text: The studies were faked
    explanation: Researchers are trying to find a way to preserve any protective factor while making milk safe. This is an honest example of **Uncertain** science that does not justify the health claims made by raw-milk advocates.
  - id: cow-urine
    prompt: What is the evidence grade for cow urine (gomutra) or panchagavya curing cancer, diabetes or infections in humans?
    options:
      - text: Established by large clinical trials
      - text: Strong
      - id: not-supported
        text: Not supported — there are no adequate human clinical trials showing such benefits
        correct: true
    explanation: The evidence base consists of laboratory and small, low-quality studies. Patents granted for cow-urine distillates are not evidence of clinical effectiveness; patents certify novelty, not that something works in patients. Religious significance is not evidence either.
  - id: urine-risk
    prompt: Which are documented health risks associated with ingesting animal urine or applying dung?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Leptospirosis can be transmitted through urine of infected animals, including cattle
        correct: true
      - text: Applying dung to a newborn's umbilical cord is a recognised cause of neonatal tetanus
        correct: true
      - text: Animal urine can contain pathogenic bacteria; a 2023 study by India's Indian Veterinary Research Institute reported harmful bacteria including E. coli in cow urine samples
        correct: true
      - text: Urine is always sterile and therefore harmless
    explanation: Urine is a waste product. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Indian medical associations publicly warned against cow dung and urine "therapies", which had no evidence of benefit.
  - id: special-pleading
    prompt: A remedy is defended with "you can't test it scientifically because it's sacred". Which reasoning error is this?
    options:
      - id: special-pleading
        text: Special pleading — exempting a claim from the standards applied to all other claims
        correct: true
      - text: Peer review
      - text: Statistical significance
    explanation: Any claim that a substance cures disease in human bodies is testable with a controlled trial, whatever its cultural or religious status. Respect for people's beliefs does not require pretending untested claims are proven.
---
## Learning objectives

- Explain why pasteurisation is one of public health's great successes
- Evaluate raw milk claims against data
- Apply the same standards to sacred and traditional remedies as to any other claim

## Why milk was pasteurised

In the 19th and early 20th centuries, milk was a leading vehicle for tuberculosis (Mycobacterium bovis),
typhoid, scarlet fever, diphtheria, brucellosis and infant diarrhoea. In the US in 1938, milk-borne outbreaks
caused about a quarter of all reported food- and water-borne outbreaks; today the share is below 1% (FDA), and
most dairy outbreaks involve unpasteurised products.

## Raw milk claims judged

| Claim | Grade | Evidence |
|-------|-------|----------|
| Raw milk carries a much higher risk of infection | **Established** | Outbreak surveillance; Costard 2017 |
| Pasteurisation substantially reduces nutritional value | **Not supported** | Small losses of vitamins C, B1, B12; milk's protein, calcium and fat are unaffected |
| Raw milk prevents lactose intolerance | **Not supported** | Mummah et al., randomised crossover trial, 2014 |
| Raw milk enzymes aid digestion | **Not supported** | Milk enzymes are digested like other proteins |
| Farm milk exposure is associated with less childhood asthma | **Uncertain** | Association in farming communities; not shown for shop-bought raw milk; not a recommendation |
| Raw milk is safe if the farm is clean | **Not supported** | Outbreaks occur at certified and "clean" farms; contamination comes from udder infection and faeces |

Groups most harmed — children, pregnant people, the elderly and the immunocompromised — are often the ones
encouraged to drink raw milk "for health".

## Sacred and traditional animal products

Many cultures attach religious or traditional significance to particular animals and their products. Such
beliefs are a matter of faith and deserve respect as beliefs. **Medical claims are different**: when someone
says a substance cures cancer, diabetes or infection, that claim is testable and must meet the same standard as
a drug.

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Cow urine or panchagavya cures cancer, diabetes, COVID-19 or other diseases | **Not supported** |
| Cow dung applied to skin or wounds protects against infection | **Not supported**; dung can carry tetanus spores |
| A product is safe because it comes from a revered animal | **Not supported** — sanctity is not sterility |
| Ingesting any animal's urine is a risk for zoonotic infection | **Strong** (leptospirosis and other pathogens) |

The same reasoning applies to rhino horn (keratin, like fingernails), bear bile, and countless other
traditional animal remedies whose demand drives species toward extinction without demonstrated benefit.

## Sources

- Costard S et al. Outbreak-related disease burden associated with consumption of unpasteurized cow's milk and cheese, United States, 2009–2014. *Emerg Infect Dis* 2017.
- Koski L et al. Foodborne illness outbreaks linked to unpasteurised milk and relationship to changes in state laws — United States, 1998–2018. *Epidemiol Infect* 2022.
- Mummah S et al. Effect of raw milk on lactose intolerance: a randomized controlled pilot study. *Ann Fam Med* 2014.
- Loss G et al. The protective effect of farm milk consumption on childhood asthma and atopy: the GABRIELA study. *J Allergy Clin Immunol* 2011.
- US FDA. Investigation of avian influenza A (H5N1) virus in dairy cattle. 2024–2025 updates.
- CDC. Raw milk: questions and answers.
- WHO. Neonatal tetanus elimination; leptospirosis fact sheets.

title: Detoxes, alkaline diets and other persistent myths
questions:
  - id: detox
    prompt: Which organs remove waste products and toxins from the body?
    options:
      - id: organs
        text: Mainly the liver and kidneys, with the lungs, gut and skin also involved
        correct: true
      - text: Juice cleanses and foot pads
      - text: Charcoal supplements taken daily
    explanation: A 2015 review found no rigorous clinical evidence that commercial detox diets eliminate toxins. Detox foot pads turn dark because of moisture and ingredients in the pad.
  - id: alkaline
    prompt: Can diet change your blood pH in a healthy person?
    options:
      - text: Yes, by a large amount
      - id: no-tight
        text: No — blood pH is held between about 7.35 and 7.45; diet can change urine pH, not blood pH
        correct: true
    explanation: Blood pH outside this range is a medical emergency (acidosis or alkalosis). The "alkaline diet" is healthy only because it encourages vegetables and fruit.
  - id: msg
    prompt: What have double-blind, placebo-controlled studies found about MSG and "Chinese restaurant syndrome"?
    options:
      - text: MSG consistently causes headaches and palpitations in most people
      - id: not-consistent
        text: They have not consistently reproduced symptoms; some people may report mild transient symptoms at large doses without food
        correct: true
      - text: MSG is banned worldwide
    explanation: Glutamate occurs naturally in tomatoes, Parmesan and human breast milk. The original 1968 "syndrome" letter and the reaction to it have been criticised as reflecting prejudice against Chinese cuisine.
  - id: late-eating
    prompt: Does eating after 8 pm cause weight gain regardless of total intake?
    options:
      - text: Yes, calories eaten late are stored as fat
      - id: total
        text: Not shown — total energy intake matters most; late eating may matter for some people because of extra snacking or effects on sleep, and the research on meal timing is still developing
        correct: true
    explanation: Grade - **Uncertain** for a specific effect of timing; **Not supported** for "late calories automatically become fat".
  - id: gluten-free
    prompt: For people without coeliac disease, wheat allergy or diagnosed sensitivity, is a gluten-free diet healthier?
    options:
      - text: Yes, gluten is toxic to everyone
      - id: no-benefit
        text: No evidence of benefit; gluten-free products are often lower in fibre and fortification and more expensive
        correct: true
    explanation: A large cohort study (Lebwohl 2017) found no link between gluten intake and heart disease in people without coeliac disease, and suggested avoiding gluten may reduce whole-grain intake.
  - id: colloidal-silver
    prompt: What is a known harm of colloidal silver supplements?
    options:
      - id: argyria
        text: Argyria — permanent blue-grey discoloration of the skin
        correct: true
      - text: There are no harms
      - text: It cures all infections
    explanation: The FDA ruled in 1999 that over-the-counter colloidal silver products are not recognised as safe and effective for any disease.
  - id: celery-juice
    prompt: Celery juice, apple cider vinegar and lemon water are widely promoted as cures. What is the general evidence grade?
    options:
      - text: Established
      - id: not-supported
        text: Not supported for disease cures; small or no effects in limited studies
        correct: true
    explanation: Apple cider vinegar has small, short-term effects on post-meal glucose in a few trials; it can erode tooth enamel and damage the oesophagus if drunk undiluted.
  - id: homeopathy
    prompt: What did Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council conclude in its 2015 review of homeopathy?
    options:
      - text: It works for most conditions
      - id: no-reliable
        text: There were no health conditions for which there was reliable evidence that homeopathy was effective
        correct: true
      - text: It is more effective than antibiotics
    explanation: Typical "30C" dilutions are so extreme that no molecule of the original substance is likely to remain. Any effect beyond placebo would contradict well-established chemistry and physics.
  - id: myths-list
    prompt: Which statements are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Microwaving does not make food radioactive
        correct: true
      - text: Eating carrots helps vision only if you are vitamin A deficient; it will not give you night vision otherwise
        correct: true
      - text: Swallowed gum is not digested but passes through, usually within days
        correct: true
      - text: Spicy food causes stomach ulcers
    explanation: Most peptic ulcers are caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID drugs — a discovery that won Marshall and Warren the 2005 Nobel Prize.

## Learning objectives

- Recognise and refute common nutrition myths
- Understand why myths persist

## Myths judged

| Claim | Grade | Note |
|-------|-------|------|
| Detox diets, teas and cleanses remove toxins | **Not supported** | The liver and kidneys do this; no "toxin" is ever named or measured |
| Alkaline diet changes blood pH and prevents cancer | **Not supported** | Fenton & Huang 2016 systematic review |
| MSG is dangerous | **Not supported** | GRAS (FDA); double-blind trials inconsistent |
| Gluten-free is healthier for everyone | **Not supported** | Essential only for coeliac disease and related conditions |
| Eating late makes you fat independent of intake | **Uncertain** to **Not supported** | |
| Carbohydrates at night are worse | **Uncertain** | |
| Frequent small meals "stoke metabolism" | **Not supported** | Thermic effect depends on total intake |
| Microwaving destroys nutrients more than other cooking | **Not supported** | Short times and little water often preserve nutrients better than boiling |
| "Negative-calorie" foods (celery) | **Not supported** | Digestion costs only a fraction of the calories |
| Colloidal silver, homeopathy, celery juice cure disease | **Not supported** | |
| Spicy food causes ulcers | **Not supported** | H. pylori and NSAIDs are the main causes |
| Egg yolks or all fat must be avoided | **Not supported** in that absolute form | |

## Why myths persist

- **Placebo, natural recovery and regression to the mean:** people try remedies when they feel worst, so
  they usually feel better afterwards regardless
- **Confirmation bias:** successes are remembered, failures forgotten
- **Commercial incentives:** an unfalsifiable product never fails a trial
- **Identity:** diets become tribal, political or religious identities, which makes evidence feel like an attack

## Sources

- Klein AV, Kiat H. Detox diets for toxin elimination and weight management: a critical review of the evidence. *J Hum Nutr Diet* 2015.
- Fenton TR, Huang T. Systematic review of the association between dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer. *BMJ Open* 2016. [doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010438](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010438)
- Geha RS et al. Review of alleged reaction to monosodium glutamate and outcome of a multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled study. *J Nutr* 2000.
- Lebwohl B et al. Long term gluten consumption in adults without celiac disease and risk of coronary heart disease. *BMJ* 2017.
- National Health and Medical Research Council (Australia). NHMRC information paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy for treating health conditions. 2015.
- US FDA. Over-the-counter drug products containing colloidal silver ingredients or silver salts. Final rule, 1999.

title: Additives, pesticides, contaminants and GMOs
questions:
  - id: dose-poison
    prompt: What does "the dose makes the poison" mean?
    options:

        correct: true
      - text: All chemicals are equally dangerous
      - text: Natural chemicals are never toxic
    explanation: Attributed to Paracelsus (16th century), it remains the foundation of toxicology.
  - id: gmo-nasem

        correct: true
      - text: It found GE foods cause cancer
      - text: It did not assess food safety
    explanation: WHO, the European Commission's research programmes and many scientific academies have reached similar conclusions. Debates about patents, corporate concentration, herbicide use and labelling are real but are economic and environmental questions, not food-safety ones.
  - id: organic
    prompt: What did the Stanford systematic review (Smith-Spangler 2012) find about organic foods?
    options:
      - text: Organic foods are much more nutritious
      - id: residues
        text: There was little evidence that organic foods are more nutritious, though they had lower pesticide residues (conventional residues were usually within safety limits)
        correct: true
      - text: Organic foods are pesticide-free by definition
    explanation: Organic farming uses approved pesticides too, including natural ones such as copper sulphate. Whether lower residue exposure improves health outcomes is **Uncertain**.
  - id: mercury
    prompt: Which fish are highest in mercury and should be avoided by pregnant people and young children?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Shark
        correct: true
      - text: Swordfish
        correct: true
      - text: King mackerel
        correct: true
      - text: Bigeye tuna
        correct: true
      - text: Sardines
    explanation: Large, long-lived predatory fish accumulate methylmercury. Sardines, salmon and anchovies are low in mercury and high in omega-3.
  - id: arsenic-rice
    prompt: How can inorganic arsenic in rice be reduced at home?
    options:
      - id: excess-water
        text: Rinsing rice and cooking it in a large excess of water, then draining, reduces arsenic substantially (with some loss of B vitamins in enriched rice)
        correct: true
      - text: It cannot be reduced
      - text: By adding more salt
    explanation: Brown rice contains more arsenic than white because arsenic concentrates in the bran. Infant rice cereal is a particular concern; the FDA set an action level of 100 ppb in 2020.
  - id: glyphosate
    prompt: Why do IARC and regulators such as the US EPA and EFSA disagree about glyphosate?
    options:
      - id: hazard-risk
        text: IARC assesses hazard (can it cause cancer under some circumstances?), while regulators assess risk at realistic exposure levels; they also weighed some studies differently
        correct: true
      - text: One of them did not look at any data
      - text: They agree completely
    explanation: IARC classified glyphosate as Group 2A (probably carcinogenic) in 2015; EPA and EFSA concluded it is unlikely to pose a carcinogenic risk at expected exposures. Grade for dietary residues causing cancer - **Uncertain**, leaning **Not supported** at normal exposure.
  - id: e-numbers
    prompt: What does an "E number" on a food label in Europe indicate?
    options:
      - text: The additive is dangerous
      - id: approved
        text: The additive has been evaluated and approved for use in the EU
        correct: true
      - text: The food is genetically modified
    explanation: E300 is vitamin C (ascorbic acid); E330 is citric acid; E948 is oxygen. Approval does not mean every additive is beyond question — titanium dioxide (E171) was withdrawn by the EU in 2022 because genotoxicity could not be ruled out.
  - id: colours
    prompt: What did the 2007 Southampton study suggest about certain artificial food colours?
    options:
      - id: hyperactivity
        text: A mix of certain artificial colours plus sodium benzoate increased hyperactive behaviour slightly in some children
        correct: true
      - text: They cause cancer
      - text: They had no effect at all
    explanation: The EU then required a warning label on six colours. The effect size was small and its clinical significance debated — grade **Uncertain**. Several US states and the FDA have since moved to phase out some petroleum-based dyes.
  - id: acrylamide
    prompt: Acrylamide forms when starchy foods are fried, roasted or baked at high temperatures. What is the state of the evidence?
    options:
      - id: animal-uncertain
        text: It is carcinogenic in animals at high doses (IARC 2A), but human dietary studies have not shown consistent cancer increases
        correct: true
      - text: It is proven to cause most cancers
      - text: It does not exist
    explanation: Reasonable precautions include not over-browning toast and chips ("go for gold"). Grade for dietary harm at normal intakes - **Uncertain**.

## Learning objectives

- Apply hazard-versus-risk thinking to chemicals in food
- Know the main contaminants that matter
- Evaluate GMO and organic claims

## How additives are regulated

Regulators (FDA, EFSA, JECFA) set an **acceptable daily intake (ADI)** — usually the highest dose with no
observed adverse effect in animal studies divided by 100. Typical consumer intakes are generally far below
ADIs. Systems are not perfect: in the US, the "self-affirmed GRAS" pathway lets companies declare an ingredient
safe without notifying the FDA, which has been criticised by researchers and policymakers.

## Contaminants that matter

| Contaminant | Main sources | Health concern | Grade |
|------------|--------------|----------------|-------|
| Methylmercury | Large predatory fish | Fetal brain development | **Established** |
| Inorganic arsenic | Rice, some well water | Cancer, development | **Strong** at high exposure |
| Lead | Old pipes, some spices, contaminated products | Child neurodevelopment, no safe level | **Established** |
| Aflatoxins | Mouldy grains and nuts | Liver cancer | **Established** |
| Acrylamide | Fried and browned starches | Animal carcinogen | **Uncertain** for humans at dietary doses |
| Microplastics | Widespread | Unknown | **Uncertain** |
| PFAS | Packaging, water | Some immune, lipid and cancer effects | **Strong** for some PFAS at high exposures; dietary contribution **Uncertain** |

Lead deserves emphasis: the 2023 US recall of cinnamon applesauce pouches after children were poisoned, and
repeated findings of lead in imported spices and some traditional medicines, show that contamination risk is
real for "natural" and traditional products too.

## Biotechnology

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Approved GM foods are as safe to eat as conventional counterparts | **Established** scientific consensus |
| GM foods cause cancer, allergies or infertility | **Not supported** |
| Organic food is more nutritious | **Not supported** in any meaningful way |
| Organic food has lower pesticide residues | **Established** |
| Lower residues produce measurable health benefits | **Uncertain** |

## Sources

- National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. *Genetically Engineered Crops: Experiences and Prospects.* 2016. [doi:10.17226/23395](https://doi.org/10.17226/23395)
- Smith-Spangler C et al. Are organic foods safer or healthier than conventional alternatives? *Ann Intern Med* 2012. [doi:10.7326/0003-4819-157-5-201209040-00007](https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-157-5-201209040-00007)
- McCann D et al. Food additives and hyperactive behaviour in 3-year-old and 8/9-year-old children (Southampton). *Lancet* 2007.
- IARC Monographs volume 112 (glyphosate), 2015; US EPA glyphosate interim decision, 2020; EFSA conclusion on glyphosate, 2023.
- EFSA. Safety assessment of titanium dioxide (E171) as a food additive. *EFSA J* 2021.
- US FDA. Inorganic arsenic in rice cereals for infants: action level guidance. 2020.
- US FDA and EPA. Advice about eating fish. 2022.

## Learning objectives

- Evaluate intermittent fasting against calorie restriction
- Judge breakfast and meal-timing claims

## Types of fasting

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| Time-restricted eating (TRE) | Eating within a 6–10 hour window daily |
| 5:2 | Two non-consecutive low-calorie days (about 500–600 kcal) each week |
| Alternate-day fasting | Fasting or very low intake every other day |
| Prolonged fasting | More than 48 hours; requires medical supervision |

## Evidence

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Intermittent fasting produces weight loss | **Established** — through reduced intake |
| It beats equal-calorie daily restriction | **Not supported** |
| It improves insulin sensitivity beyond weight loss | **Uncertain** (some early TRE studies suggest yes) |
| Fasting extends human lifespan | **Uncertain** — animal data only |
| Breakfast is needed for weight control | **Not supported** |
| Eating in line with circadian rhythm (earlier in the day) is metabolically favourable | **Uncertain** to **Strong** for glucose; outcome data lacking |

## Sources

- Liu D et al. Calorie restriction with or without time-restricted eating in weight loss. *NEJM* 2022. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2114833](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2114833)
- Trepanowski JF et al. Effect of alternate-day fasting on weight loss, weight maintenance, and cardioprotection. *JAMA Intern Med* 2017. [doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.0936](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.0936)
- Lowe DA et al. Effects of time-restricted eating on weight loss and other metabolic parameters (TREAT). *JAMA Intern Med* 2020. [doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.4153](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.4153)
- Sievert K et al. Effect of breakfast on weight and energy intake: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. *BMJ* 2019. [doi:10.1136/bmj.l42](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l42)
- Sutton EF et al. Early time-restricted feeding improves insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and oxidative stress even without weight loss in men with prediabetes. *Cell Metab* 2018.

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish allergy, autoimmune disease and intolerance
- Know validated diagnostic approaches
- Recognise invalid tests

## Comparison

| Condition | Mechanism | Diagnosis | Treatment |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| IgE food allergy | Immune (IgE) | History plus skin-prick or specific IgE; oral food challenge | Avoidance, adrenaline auto-injector; oral immunotherapy for some |
| Coeliac disease | Autoimmune | tTG-IgA blood test and intestinal biopsy, on a gluten-containing diet | Lifelong strict gluten-free diet |
| Lactose intolerance | Low lactase enzyme | Clinical history; hydrogen breath test | Limit lactose; lactase enzymes; lactose-free products |
| IBS (FODMAP-sensitive) | Gut sensitivity, motility | Clinical criteria (Rome IV) | Low-FODMAP diet with reintroduction, among others |
| Non-coeliac gluten/wheat sensitivity | Unclear | Exclusion of coeliac and wheat allergy | Individual trial of reduction |

## Invalid tests

Applied kinesiology, hair analysis, IgG food panels, electrodermal ("Vega") testing and pulse tests have no
diagnostic validity for food allergy or intolerance. Grade - **Not supported**.

## Sources

- Skodje GI et al. Fructan, rather than gluten, induces symptoms in patients with self-reported non-celiac gluten sensitivity. *Gastroenterology* 2018. [doi:10.1053/j.gastro.2017.10.040](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2017.10.040)
- Muraro A et al. EAACI guideline: anaphylaxis (2021 update). *Allergy* 2022.
- Rubio-Tapia A et al. ACG guidelines update: diagnosis and management of celiac disease. *Am J Gastroenterol* 2023.
- Stapel SO et al. Testing for IgG4 against foods is not recommended as a diagnostic tool: EAACI task force report. *Allergy* 2008.
- US FDA. Food Allergy Safety, Treatment, Education, and Research (FASTER) Act of 2021.

## Learning objectives

- Summarise the book's main conclusions by certainty
- Distinguish genuine scientific uncertainty from manufactured doubt

## Established

- Energy balance governs body-fat change; expenditure falls as weight falls
- Deficiency diseases: vitamin C (scurvy), thiamin (beriberi), niacin (pellagra), vitamin D (rickets), B12, iodine,
  iron, vitamin A
- Folic acid prevents neural tube defects; vitamin K at birth prevents bleeding; vegans need B12
- LDL cholesterol causes atherosclerosis; saturated fat raises LDL relative to unsaturated fat
- Industrial trans fats cause heart disease
- Sodium raises blood pressure; DASH lowers it
- Alcohol causes cancer and other harms with dose
- Processed meat causes colorectal cancer (small absolute risk)
- Free sugars cause tooth decay
- Lifestyle change prevents type 2 diabetes in high-risk adults; major weight loss can induce remission
- Pasteurisation prevents milk-borne disease; raw milk carries much higher infection risk
- High-dose beta-carotene increases lung cancer in smokers
- Early peanut introduction reduces peanut allergy in high-risk infants
- Approved GM foods are as safe as conventional foods

## Strong

- High fibre and whole grain intake lowers chronic-disease risk
- Mediterranean-style patterns reduce cardiovascular events
- Sugary drinks promote weight gain and type 2 diabetes
- Fruit, vegetables, legumes and nuts are associated with lower mortality
- Replacing red and processed meat with plant protein lowers risk
- Higher protein helps older adults and people losing weight retain muscle
- Moderate coffee and tea are safe for most adults
- Ultra-processed foods are associated with poor outcomes and can drive overeating

## Uncertain

- Health effects of eggs at moderate intake
- Effects of full-fat versus low-fat dairy
- Long-term effects of sweeteners and emulsifiers
- Role of the gut microbiome in most diseases; probiotics for healthy people
- Benefits of meal timing and fasting beyond calorie reduction
- Optimal vitamin D level; effect on cancer mortality
- Very-low-dose alcohol effects on total mortality
- Precise mechanisms of ultra-processed food harm
- Whether a defended body-weight "set point" exists
- Long-term safety of lifelong GLP-1 therapy

## Not supported

- Detoxes, cleanses, alkaline diets, blood-type diets
- Raw milk health claims
- Cow urine, dung and other sacred-animal medical remedies
- Diet cures for cancer or type 1 diabetes
- Antioxidant supplements for disease prevention
- Seed-oil toxicity at normal intakes
- MSG and sugar-hyperactivity scares
- Homeopathy, colloidal silver, IgG food-intolerance tests

## Sources

This chapter summarises the sources cited in previous chapters.

## Learning objectives

- Translate evidence into daily eating
- Read a nutrition label efficiently

## A practical summary

1. **Eat mostly plants** — vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts and seeds
2. **Choose fats well** — prefer olive, canola and other vegetable oils over butter, lard and tallow
3. **Pick protein sources thoughtfully** — legumes, fish, poultry, dairy and eggs; little processed meat
4. **Drink water** — limit sugary drinks; less alcohol is better, none is best for cancer risk
5. **Watch salt** — most comes from packaged and restaurant food
6. **Cook more, from minimally processed ingredients**, when you can
7. **Keep food safe** — pasteurised dairy, thorough cooking, cold storage
8. **Supplement only for a reason** — folic acid in pre-conception, B12 for vegans, vitamin D for infants and at-risk groups
9. **Ignore miracle claims** — no single food, ritual or product saves or ruins your health
10. **Find a pattern you can sustain** — adherence beats perfection

## Reading a label, in order

1. Serving size and servings per container
2. Calories per serving
3. Added sugars, sodium and saturated fat (lower is better)
4. Fibre (higher is better)
5. The ingredients list (first few ingredients make up most of the product)

## Sources

- Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Healthy Eating Plate.
- Public Health England. The Eatwell Guide. 2016.
- US FDA. How to understand and use the Nutrition Facts label.
- WHO. Healthy diet fact sheet.
- Drewnowski A. The cost of US foods as related to their nutritive value. *Am J Clin Nutr* 2010.

title: Cumulative review quiz
questions:
  - id: r-kcal
    prompt: A snack contains 10 g protein, 20 g carbohydrate and 10 g fat. Approximately how many kcal does it provide?
    options:
      - text: 160 kcal
      - id: two-ten
        text: 210 kcal
        correct: true
      - text: 400 kcal
    explanation: (10 × 4) + (20 × 4) + (10 × 9) = 40 + 80 + 90 = 210 kcal.
  - id: r-design
    prompt: Which design can best establish that a diet causes a reduction in heart attacks?
    options:
      - text: A cross-sectional survey
      - text: A case report
      - id: rct

        correct: true
    explanation: Converging evidence from cohorts and genetics adds confidence, but randomisation is the strongest single tool for causation.
  - id: r-nnt

      - text: 20%

        correct: true

| Vitamin D | 600 IU adults (RDA); 400 IU breastfed infants |

title: Why design principles matter
questions:
  - id: cost-of-change
    prompt: What is the main problem that design principles such as SOLID try to address?
    options:
      - id: change
        text: Keeping the cost of changing software low as it grows
        correct: true
      - text: Making programs run faster on modern hardware
      - text: Reducing the number of classes in a codebase
      - text: Replacing the need for automated tests
    explanation: Most of a system's lifetime cost is change. SOLID is about structuring code so that changes stay local, predictable and cheap.
  - id: coupling-cohesion
    prompt: Which combination usually indicates a healthy design?
    options:
      - id: low-high
        text: Low coupling and high cohesion
        correct: true
      - text: High coupling and high cohesion
      - text: High coupling and low cohesion
      - text: Low coupling and low cohesion
    explanation: Modules should depend on each other as little as possible (low coupling) while the code inside each module should be strongly related (high cohesion).
  - id: rigidity-symptoms
    prompt: Which of these are symptoms of a rotting design?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: A small change forces edits in many unrelated places
        correct: true
      - text: Fixing a bug in one module breaks behaviour in another
        correct: true
      - text: A useful module cannot be reused because it drags in too many dependencies
        correct: true
      - text: The codebase has a comprehensive automated test suite
    explanation: Rigidity, fragility and immobility are the classic symptoms described by Robert C. Martin. A good test suite is a sign of health, not rot.
  - id: solid-origin
    prompt: Who coined the acronym "SOLID" for the principles popularised by Robert C. Martin?
    options:
      - text: Barbara Liskov
      - text: Bertrand Meyer
      - id: feathers
        text: Michael Feathers
        correct: true
      - text: Kent Beck
    explanation: Robert C. Martin described the principles around 2000; Michael Feathers later noticed the letters spelled SOLID.
---
Software rarely fails because it cannot be written. It fails because, after a few years, it can
no longer be **changed** safely. Design principles are a vocabulary for keeping change cheap.

## Learning objectives

- Explain coupling and cohesion and why they matter
- Recognise the symptoms of a design that resists change
- Name the five SOLID principles and their origins

## Coupling and cohesion

**Coupling** measures how much one module knows about another. **Cohesion** measures how
closely the responsibilities inside one module belong together.

```csharp
public class ReportService
{
    public string Build(Order order)
    {
        var connection = new SqlConnection("Server=prod;...");
        var smtp = new SmtpClient("mail.example.com");
        // query the database, format HTML, send e-mail, write a log file...
        return "done";
    }
}
```

This class is tightly coupled to SQL Server, SMTP and the file system, and it has low cohesion:
data access, formatting and delivery are unrelated jobs. Any change in any of those areas touches
this one class, and none of it can be tested without real infrastructure.

## Symptoms of rot

Robert C. Martin described four smells of a decaying design:

| Symptom | What it feels like |
|---------|--------------------|
| Rigidity | Every change cascades into many other changes |
| Fragility | Changes break things in places that seem unrelated |
| Immobility | Useful parts cannot be reused elsewhere |
| Viscosity | Doing the right thing is harder than hacking around it |

## The five principles

| Letter | Principle | One-line idea |
|--------|-----------|---------------|
| S | Single Responsibility | A module should have one reason to change |
| O | Open/Closed | Extend behaviour without modifying existing code |
| L | Liskov Substitution | Subtypes must be usable wherever their base type is expected |
| I | Interface Segregation | Clients should not depend on methods they do not use |
| D | Dependency Inversion | Depend on abstractions, not on concrete details |

The principles were collected by Robert C. Martin around 2000; Michael Feathers noticed the
acronym. Liskov substitution comes from Barbara Liskov (1987) and open/closed from Bertrand Meyer (1988).

> Principles are heuristics, not laws. Each chapter ends with the cost of applying the principle,
> because over-applying SOLID creates its own kind of rigidity.

---
title: Abstractions and polymorphism in C#
questions:
  - id: interface-vs-abstract
    prompt: Which statement about C# interfaces and abstract classes is correct?
    options:
      - text: A class can inherit from several abstract classes
      - text: Interfaces cannot declare methods with a body in modern C#
      - id: multi-interface
        text: A class can implement many interfaces but inherit from only one class
        correct: true
      - text: Abstract classes cannot contain implemented methods
    explanation: C# has single class inheritance and multiple interface implementation. Since C# 8, interfaces may also contain default implementations.
  - id: polymorphism
    prompt: What does polymorphism let a caller do?
    options:
      - id: same-call
        text: Use one call site that behaves differently depending on the runtime type of the object
        correct: true
      - text: Call private methods of another class
      - text: Avoid declaring types for variables
    explanation: The caller depends only on the abstraction; the concrete type decides what actually happens.
  - id: good-abstraction
    prompt: Which are signs of a good abstraction?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It is named after what callers need, not after how it is implemented
        correct: true
      - text: It exposes implementation details such as SQL connection strings
      - text: Several different implementations could reasonably satisfy it
        correct: true
      - text: It is small enough to be understood quickly
        correct: true
    explanation: Good abstractions are expressed in the caller's language, hide details and are small enough to implement in more than one way.
---
Every SOLID principle relies on two language features: **abstractions** (interfaces and abstract
classes) and **polymorphism** (calling through an abstraction and letting the runtime type decide).

## Learning objectives

- Choose between an interface and an abstract class
- Use polymorphism to remove type-checking conditionals
- Recognise what makes an abstraction useful

## Interfaces and abstract classes

```csharp
public interface IClock
{
    DateTimeOffset UtcNow { get; }
}

public abstract class Shape
{
    public abstract double Area();
    public override string ToString() => $"{GetType().Name} with area {Area():F2}";
}

public sealed class Circle(double radius) : Shape
{
    public override double Area() => Math.PI * radius * radius;
}
```

| Use an interface when… | Use an abstract class when… |
|------------------------|-----------------------------|
| You describe a capability (`IComparable`, `IDisposable`) | You share real implementation between related types |
| Unrelated types may implement it | Types form a genuine "is-a" family |
| You want a type to have several roles | You need constructors or protected state |

Since C# 8, interfaces may carry **default interface methods**, but they are best kept for
evolving published interfaces, not as a substitute for base classes.

## Polymorphism replaces conditionals

```csharp
double TotalArea(IEnumerable<Shape> shapes) => shapes.Sum(s => s.Area());
```

Compare that with a version that switches on a `Kind` property: every new shape forces a change
to every switch. Polymorphism moves the varying behaviour into the type that owns it.

## What makes a good abstraction

- It is named after the caller's need (`IOrderRepository`, `IClock`), not the technology (`ISqlHelper`)
- It is small — callers can understand it at a glance
- More than one implementation is plausible (including a test double)

> .NET 8 introduced `TimeProvider`, a built-in abstraction for time. Prefer it over hand-rolled
> `IClock` interfaces in new code.

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/02-single-responsibility/01-one-reason-to-change.md

---
title: One reason to change
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: In Robert C. Martin's refined wording, a module should be responsible to how many actors?
    options:
      - text: None
      - text: As many as needed, as long as the class is short
      - id: one
        text: One
        correct: true
      - text: Two — the developer and the user
    explanation: "\"A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor.\" An actor is a group of stakeholders who would request changes for the same reason."
  - id: misconception
    prompt: Which statement about SRP is a misconception?
    options:
      - id: one-method
        text: Every class should have exactly one method
        correct: true
      - text: Code that changes for different reasons should be separated
      - text: Code that changes for the same reason should be kept together
    explanation: SRP is about reasons to change, not about counting methods. A cohesive class can have many methods serving one actor.
  - id: actors
    prompt: "An `Employee` class has `CalculatePay()` (used by finance), `ReportHours()` (used by operations) and `Save()` (owned by the DBA team). Which statements are true?"
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: The class serves three different actors
        correct: true
      - text: A change requested by finance could accidentally break the operations report
        correct: true
      - text: The class satisfies SRP because each method is short
      - text: Splitting by actor reduces the chance of accidental coupling
        correct: true
    explanation: This is Martin's own example. Three actors means three reasons to change living in one class.
---
The **Single Responsibility Principle** is the most quoted and most misunderstood SOLID principle.

## Learning objectives

- State SRP in terms of actors and reasons to change
- Identify mixed responsibilities in a class
- Avoid the "one method per class" misreading

## The definition

The original wording was *"a class should have only one reason to change."* Martin later sharpened
it: **a module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor.** An actor is a group of people
— finance, operations, a compliance team — who request changes for the same reason.

## A class with three masters

```csharp
public class Employee
{
    public decimal CalculatePay() { /* rules owned by finance */ return 0; }
    public string ReportHours()   { /* format owned by operations */ return ""; }
    public void Save()            { /* schema owned by the DBA team */ }
}
```

Suppose `CalculatePay` and `ReportHours` share a private helper `RegularHours()`. Finance asks
for a change to how overtime is counted, a developer updates the helper, and the operations
report silently changes too. Nobody asked for that.

## Separating by actor

```csharp
public sealed record EmployeeData(int Id, string Name, IReadOnlyList<TimeEntry> Entries);

public sealed class PayCalculator      { public decimal Calculate(EmployeeData e) => 0; }
public sealed class HoursReporter      { public string Report(EmployeeData e) => ""; }
public sealed class EmployeeRepository { public Task SaveAsync(EmployeeData e) => Task.CompletedTask; }
```

Each class now changes for one reason. The shared data is a plain record with no behaviour that
could couple the actors together.

## Finding responsibilities

Useful questions when reviewing a class:

- Who would ask for this code to change? If the answer is several unrelated groups, split.
- Does the class name need "And" or "Manager" to describe it?
- Do its tests need very different kinds of setup (a database *and* an SMTP server)?

> SRP applies at every level: functions, classes, modules and services. The same reasoning that
> splits a class also tells you where to draw microservice boundaries.

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/02-single-responsibility/02-refactoring-to-srp.md

---
title: Refactoring toward SRP
questions:
  - id: first-step
    prompt: Before splitting a large class with mixed responsibilities, what should you have in place?
    options:
      - text: A new database schema
      - text: A microservice for each responsibility
      - id: tests
        text: Tests that pin down its current behaviour
        correct: true
      - text: A dependency injection container
    explanation: Characterisation tests let you refactor with confidence that behaviour has not changed.
  - id: facade
    prompt: After extracting responsibilities, existing callers still call `OrderProcessor.Process`. What is the role of `OrderProcessor` now?
    options:
      - text: It is dead code that should be deleted
      - id: coordinator
        text: A thin coordinator that delegates to focused collaborators
        correct: true
      - text: A violation of SRP because it calls several classes
    explanation: Orchestrating focused collaborators is itself a single responsibility — the workflow.
  - id: over-split
    prompt: Which are risks of splitting responsibilities too aggressively?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Logic that always changes together ends up scattered across many files
        correct: true
      - text: Readers must jump through many tiny classes to understand one behaviour
        correct: true
      - text: The compiler refuses to build classes with fewer than three methods
    explanation: Over-splitting lowers cohesion. Keep together what changes together.
---
Knowing the principle is easy; applying it to a 900-line class is the real skill.

## Learning objectives

- Refactor a mixed-responsibility class in small, safe steps
- Keep an orchestrating class thin
- Recognise when splitting has gone too far

## The starting point

```csharp
public class OrderProcessor
{
    public async Task ProcessAsync(Order order)
    {
        if (order.Lines.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Empty order");
        var total = order.Lines.Sum(l => l.Price * l.Quantity);
        if (order.Customer.IsVip) total *= 0.9m;

        await using var connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
        await connection.ExecuteAsync("INSERT INTO Orders ...", new { order.Id, total });

        using var smtp = new SmtpClient("mail.example.com");
        await smtp.SendMailAsync("shop@example.com", order.Customer.Email, "Thanks", $"Total {total}");
    }
}
```

Validation, pricing, persistence and notification all live together.

## Step 1 — pin the behaviour

Write characterisation tests around `ProcessAsync` (with a test database or by first extracting
seams). Refactoring without tests is just editing.

## Step 2 — extract one responsibility at a time

```csharp
public interface IPricingPolicy { decimal Total(Order order); }
public interface IOrderRepository { Task AddAsync(Order order, decimal total, CancellationToken ct); }
public interface IOrderNotifier { Task OrderPlacedAsync(Order order, decimal total, CancellationToken ct); }

public sealed class OrderProcessor(
    IPricingPolicy pricing,
    IOrderRepository orders,
    IOrderNotifier notifier)
{
    public async Task ProcessAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        OrderValidator.EnsureValid(order);
        var total = pricing.Total(order);
        await orders.AddAsync(order, total, ct);
        await notifier.OrderPlacedAsync(order, total, ct);
    }
}
```

`OrderProcessor` still exists, but its only job is the **workflow**. Each collaborator can be
tested and replaced on its own.

## Knowing when to stop

Stop splitting when the pieces would always change together. A `PricingPolicy` that contains the
VIP discount, the volume discount and rounding rules is cohesive: all of it belongs to the people
who own pricing.

> Rule of thumb: separate code that changes for different reasons; keep together code that
> changes for the same reason. Both halves of the rule matter.

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/03-open-closed/01-open-for-extension.md

---
title: Open for extension, closed for modification
questions:
  - id: meaning
    prompt: What does "closed for modification" mean in practice?
    options:
      - text: The source file is marked read-only in source control
      - text: The class must be declared `sealed`
      - text: The code can never be changed, even to fix bugs
      - id: no-edit
        text: Adding a new variant of behaviour should not require editing existing, tested code
        correct: true
    explanation: Bugs still get fixed. OCP is about extending behaviour by adding new code rather than repeatedly editing a central switch.
  - id: smell
    prompt: Which code shape most often signals an OCP violation?
    options:
      - text: A class with a primary constructor
      - text: An interface with a single method
      - id: switch
        text: A `switch` on a type code that is duplicated across several methods
        correct: true
    explanation: Every new type code forces edits to every copy of the switch. Polymorphism or a lookup of strategies removes that.
  - id: meyer
    prompt: Who first formulated the open/closed principle?
    options:
      - text: Barbara Liskov, in a 1987 keynote
      - id: meyer
        text: Bertrand Meyer, in Object-Oriented Software Construction (1988)
        correct: true
      - text: Martin Fowler, in Refactoring (1999)
    explanation: Meyer described it using inheritance; Robert C. Martin later reframed it around abstractions and polymorphism.
  - id: mechanisms
    prompt: Which C# mechanisms can make code open for extension?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Interfaces with multiple implementations
        correct: true
      - text: Delegates such as `Func<T, TResult>` passed in by the caller
        correct: true
      - text: Registering implementations in a dependency injection container
        correct: true
      - text: Copying the class and editing the copy
    explanation: Interfaces, delegates and DI registrations all let you add behaviour without touching existing code. Copy-and-edit duplicates code instead.
---
## Learning objectives

- Explain the open/closed principle and its history
- Replace type-code switches with polymorphism
- Choose the right extension point instead of making everything pluggable

## The problem

```csharp
public decimal Shipping(Order order) => order.Method switch
{
    "standard" => 4.99m,
    "express"  => 14.99m,
    "pickup"   => 0m,
    _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(order))
};
```

On its own this is fine. It becomes a problem when the same `switch` appears in `EstimatedDays`,
`Label` and `CanShipTo`. Adding "drone" means finding and editing every copy.

## Making it open

```csharp
public interface IShippingMethod
{
    string Code { get; }
    decimal Cost(Order order);
    int EstimatedDays(Address destination);
}

public sealed class ExpressShipping : IShippingMethod
{
    public string Code => "express";
    public decimal Cost(Order order) => 14.99m;
    public int EstimatedDays(Address destination) => 1;
}

public sealed class ShippingCalculator(IEnumerable<IShippingMethod> methods)
{
    private readonly Dictionary<string, IShippingMethod> _byCode =
        methods.ToDictionary(m => m.Code, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

    public decimal Cost(Order order) =>
        _byCode.TryGetValue(order.Method, out var method)
            ? method.Cost(order)
            : throw new UnknownShippingMethodException(order.Method);
}
```

Adding drone delivery is now a new class plus one registration:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IShippingMethod, DroneShipping>();
```

`ShippingCalculator` is **closed**: it never changes. The system is **open**: it gains behaviour.

## Strategic closure

No design is closed against every change. Predict which axis is likely to vary — new shipping
methods, new report formats — and make *that* axis open. Wait for the second or third real
variation before introducing the abstraction; until then, a simple `switch` is easier to read.

title: Strategies, decorators and pipelines
questions:
  - id: decorator
    prompt: You need to add caching to an existing `IProductRepository` without editing it. Which pattern fits best?
    options:
      - text: Singleton
      - text: Abstract factory
      - id: decorator
        text: Decorator
        correct: true
      - text: Visitor
    explanation: A decorator implements the same interface, wraps the original and adds behaviour before or after delegating.
  - id: pipeline
    prompt: Which ASP.NET Core feature is an example of the open/closed principle?
    options:
      - id: middleware
        text: The middleware pipeline, where new behaviour is added with `app.Use...` calls
        correct: true
      - text: Hard-coding authentication inside every controller action
      - text: The `web.config` file
    explanation: New middleware extends request processing without modifying the framework or existing middleware.
  - id: strategy-facts
    prompt: Which statements about the strategy pattern are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface
        correct: true
      - text: In C#, a simple strategy can be a delegate such as `Func<Order, decimal>`
        correct: true
      - text: It requires inheritance from a common abstract base class
    explanation: An interface or a delegate is enough; no base class is needed.
---
## Learning objectives

- Apply the strategy and decorator patterns to achieve OCP
- Recognise pipeline-style extensibility in .NET
- Use delegates when an interface would be overkill

## Strategy

A strategy is an interchangeable algorithm. In modern C#, a delegate is often the lightest strategy:

```csharp
public sealed class PriceCalculator(Func<Order, decimal> discount)
{
    public decimal Total(Order order) => order.Subtotal - discount(order);
}

var blackFriday = new PriceCalculator(o => o.Subtotal * 0.25m);
var none = new PriceCalculator(_ => 0m);
```

Use an interface when the strategy has several members, needs dependencies, or deserves a name.

## Decorator

A decorator wraps an implementation of the same interface:

```csharp
public sealed class CachedProductRepository(IProductRepository inner, IMemoryCache cache)
    : IProductRepository
{
    public async Task<Product?> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct) =>
        await cache.GetOrCreateAsync($"product:{id}", _ => inner.GetAsync(id, ct));
}
```

The original repository is unchanged, and caching can be removed by changing one registration.
Cross-cutting concerns — caching, logging, retries, metrics — are natural decorators.

## Pipelines

ASP.NET Core's middleware is OCP at framework scale:

```csharp
app.UseExceptionHandler();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.Response.Headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff";
    await next(context);
});
```

Each `Use` adds behaviour around the next step. The same idea appears in `HttpClient`
`DelegatingHandler`s and in MediatR-style pipeline behaviours.

> Patterns are tools for OCP, not goals. If only one implementation will ever exist, the
> abstraction adds indirection without paying for itself.

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/04-liskov-substitution/01-behavioural-subtyping.md

---
title: Behavioural subtyping
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle require?
    options:
      - text: Every subclass must override every virtual method
      - text: Subclasses must not add new methods
      - id: substitutable
        text: Objects of a subtype must be usable wherever the base type is expected without breaking the program's correctness
        correct: true
      - text: A base class must know about all of its subclasses
    explanation: LSP is about behaviour. Code written against the base type must keep working when handed any subtype.
  - id: contracts
    prompt: According to design-by-contract rules for subtypes, which are correct?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: A subtype must not strengthen preconditions
        correct: true
      - text: A subtype must not weaken postconditions
        correct: true
      - text: A subtype must preserve the invariants of the base type
        correct: true
      - text: A subtype may throw new kinds of exceptions that callers of the base type do not expect
    explanation: Subtypes may demand less and promise more, never the reverse. Unexpected exceptions break callers.
  - id: square
    prompt: "Why is `Square : Rectangle` (with settable `Width` and `Height`) a classic LSP violation?"
    options:
      - text: Squares have fewer sides than rectangles
      - id: setter
        text: Code that sets width and height independently, then checks the area, breaks for a square
        correct: true
      - text: C# does not allow a class to inherit from a class with properties
    explanation: A mutable square must keep width equal to height, which violates the rectangle's implicit promise that the two vary independently.
  - id: year
    prompt: When did Barbara Liskov introduce the idea in a keynote titled "Data Abstraction and Hierarchy"?
    options:
      - text: "1972"
      - id: y1987
        text: "1987"
        correct: true
      - text: "2000"
    explanation: The 1987 OOPSLA keynote introduced it; Liskov and Jeannette Wing formalised it in 1994.
---
## Learning objectives

- State LSP and its contract rules
- Spot "is-a" relationships that are not behaviourally substitutable
- Use tests to verify substitutability

## The principle

Barbara Liskov introduced the idea in 1987. Informally: **if code works with a base type, it must
keep working with any subtype.** "Is-a" in the real world is not enough — the subtype must keep
the base type's *behavioural* promises.

## The rectangle and the square

```csharp
public class Rectangle
{
    public virtual int Width { get; set; }
    public virtual int Height { get; set; }
    public int Area => Width * Height;
}

public class Square : Rectangle
{
    public override int Width  { set { base.Width = value; base.Height = value; } }
    public override int Height { set { base.Width = value; base.Height = value; } }
}

void Resize(Rectangle r)
{
    r.Width = 5;
    r.Height = 4;
    Debug.Assert(r.Area == 20);
}
```

`Resize(new Square())` produces an area of 16. Geometrically a square *is* a rectangle; as a
**mutable** object it does not honour the rectangle's contract.

The fix is to not model it with inheritance — for example, immutable records with a shared
`IShape` interface:

```csharp
public interface IShape { double Area { get; } }
public sealed record Rect(double Width, double Height) : IShape { public double Area => Width * Height; }
public sealed record Sq(double Side) : IShape { public double Area => Side * Side; }
```

## The contract rules

| Rule | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| Preconditions cannot be strengthened | A subtype cannot demand more from callers |
| Postconditions cannot be weakened | A subtype cannot promise less |
| Invariants must be preserved | What is always true of the base stays true |
| No new unexpected exceptions | Callers should not need to catch surprises |
| History constraint | A subtype cannot allow state changes the base forbids |

## Testing substitutability

Write the base type's contract as an abstract test class and run it against every implementation:

```csharp
public abstract class ShapeContractTests
{
    protected abstract IShape Create();

    [Fact]
    public void Area_is_never_negative() => Assert.True(Create().Area >= 0);
}

public sealed class RectTests : ShapeContractTests { protected override IShape Create() => new Rect(2, 3); }
```

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/04-liskov-substitution/02-lsp-in-dotnet.md

---
title: LSP in the .NET libraries
questions:
  - id: readonly-collection
    prompt: "`ReadOnlyCollection<T>` implements `ICollection<T>`. What happens when you call `Add` on it through the `ICollection<T>` interface?"
    options:
      - text: The item is added silently
      - id: throws
        text: It throws `NotSupportedException`
        correct: true
      - text: It does nothing and returns false
      - text: It fails to compile
    explanation: "The interface promises `Add`, but the implementation refuses it. Callers must check `IsReadOnly` — a widely cited LSP smell in the BCL."
  - id: stream
    prompt: How does `System.IO.Stream` reduce surprises for callers when not every stream supports every operation?
    options:
      - text: It forbids subclasses from throwing any exception
      - text: It provides separate abstract classes for every combination of capabilities
      - id: capability
        text: It exposes capability properties such as `CanRead`, `CanWrite` and `CanSeek` as part of its contract
        correct: true
    explanation: Because the capability checks are part of the documented contract, a caller who honours them is not surprised. Splitting into smaller interfaces would be the ISP-style alternative.
  - id: fixes
    prompt: Which are good ways to fix a subtype that cannot support an inherited operation?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Split the base interface so the subtype only implements what it supports
        correct: true
      - text: Replace inheritance with composition
        correct: true
      - text: Override the method to throw `NotImplementedException` and hope nobody calls it
    explanation: Throwing from an inherited member pushes the problem onto every caller. Narrower interfaces or composition remove it at the source.
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognise LSP trade-offs in the base class library
- Distinguish "refused bequest" from legitimate capability checks
- Fix violations with narrower interfaces or composition

## A famous compromise

```csharp
ICollection<int> numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 }.AsReadOnly();
numbers.Add(4); // NotSupportedException
```

`ICollection<T>` has an `IsReadOnly` property, so technically the contract allows refusal. In
practice, many callers never check it, which is why later versions of .NET added
`IReadOnlyCollection<T>` and `IReadOnlyList<T>`. Prefer those in your own APIs:

```csharp
public IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines => _lines;
```

## Capability properties

`Stream` exposes `CanRead`, `CanWrite`, `CanSeek` and `CanTimeout`. A network stream throws
`NotSupportedException` from `Seek`, but only after declaring `CanSeek == false`. Code that
honours the capability flags keeps working with any stream, so the contract holds.

## Refused bequest

When a subclass inherits a member it does not want and throws from it, that is a **refused
bequest**:

```csharp
public class Bird { public virtual void Fly() { } }
public class Penguin : Bird
{
    public override void Fly() => throw new NotSupportedException();
}
```

## Fixing it

```csharp
public abstract class Bird { public abstract void Eat(); }
public interface IFlyer { void Fly(); }

public sealed class Sparrow : Bird, IFlyer { public override void Eat() { } public void Fly() { } }
public sealed class Penguin : Bird { public override void Eat() { } }
```

Code that needs flight asks for `IFlyer`. The compiler now prevents the bug that the exception
used to report at runtime — and that is LSP and ISP working together.

title: Client-specific interfaces
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: What does the Interface Segregation Principle state?
    options:
      - text: Every class must implement exactly one interface
      - id: clients
        text: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use
        correct: true
      - text: Interfaces must live in a separate assembly from their implementations
      - text: Interfaces should never inherit from other interfaces
    explanation: Fat interfaces couple clients to members they never call, so changes to those members ripple into unrelated clients.
  - id: who-owns
    prompt: Who should an interface be shaped around?
    options:
      - text: The class that implements it
      - text: The database schema
      - id: client
        text: The client that uses it
        correct: true
    explanation: Interfaces describe what a client needs. One implementation can satisfy several client-shaped interfaces.
  - id: symptoms
    prompt: Which are symptoms of a fat interface?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Implementations throw `NotImplementedException` for several members
        correct: true
      - text: Test doubles must stub many methods the test never touches
        correct: true
      - text: Most clients call only a small subset of the members
        correct: true
      - text: The interface has a descriptive name
    explanation: Unused members show up as stubs, throwing implementations and clients that only use a slice of the interface.
---
## Learning objectives

- State the interface segregation principle
- Split a fat interface into role interfaces
- Let one class implement several small interfaces

## A fat interface

```csharp
public interface IMultiFunctionDevice
{
    void Print(Document d);
    void Scan(Document d);
    void Fax(Document d);
    void Staple(Document d);
}

public sealed class BasicPrinter : IMultiFunctionDevice
{
    public void Print(Document d) { /* ... */ }
    public void Scan(Document d)   => throw new NotImplementedException();
    public void Fax(Document d)    => throw new NotImplementedException();
    public void Staple(Document d) => throw new NotImplementedException();
}
```

`BasicPrinter` is forced to lie, and every client that only prints still recompiles and redeploys
whenever the fax signature changes.

## Segregated interfaces

```csharp
public interface IPrinter { void Print(Document d); }
public interface IScanner { void Scan(Document d); }
public interface IFax     { void Fax(Document d); }

public sealed class BasicPrinter : IPrinter { public void Print(Document d) { } }
public sealed class OfficeMachine : IPrinter, IScanner, IFax
{
    public void Print(Document d) { }
    public void Scan(Document d) { }
    public void Fax(Document d) { }
}
```

The same `OfficeMachine` instance can be registered under several interfaces:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<OfficeMachine>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IPrinter>(sp => sp.GetRequiredService<OfficeMachine>());
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IScanner>(sp => sp.GetRequiredService<OfficeMachine>());
```

## ISP and LSP

Fat interfaces tend to cause LSP violations, because implementations throw for members they cannot
support. Segregation removes the temptation: if you cannot fax, you simply do not implement `IFax`.

## Learning objectives

- Split repositories and services by how they are used
- Recognise role interfaces in the base class library

## Read and write roles

```csharp
public interface IOrderReader
{
    Task<OrderDto?> FindAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct);
    Task<IReadOnlyList<OrderSummary>> ListForCustomerAsync(int customerId, CancellationToken ct);
}

public interface IOrderWriter
{
    Task<int> AddAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct);
    Task CancelAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct);
}

public sealed class SqlOrderStore : IOrderReader, IOrderWriter { /* ... */ }
```

The reporting page asks for `IOrderReader`. It cannot accidentally write, and its tests only need
a fake with two methods.

## Interfaces in the base class library

The BCL is full of tiny role interfaces: `IDisposable` (one method), `IAsyncDisposable`,
`IComparable<T>`, `IEquatable<T>`, `IEnumerable<T>`. Their smallness is exactly why so many types
can implement them and so much generic code can rely on them.

## Interfaces shaped for consumers

```csharp
public sealed class InvoiceEmailer(IOrderReader orders, IEmailSender email)
{
    public async Task SendAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await orders.FindAsync(orderId, ct) ?? throw new OrderNotFoundException(orderId);
        await email.SendAsync(order.CustomerEmail, "Your invoice", InvoiceTemplate.Render(order), ct);
    }
}
```

## Balance

Do not create an interface per method by reflex. Group members by the clients that use them
together. A good test: could you describe the interface's role in a short noun phrase —
"order reader", "email sender"? If so, it is probably the right size.
